articles.title: Most Americans think Trump is using presidency to enrich himself, poll finds
articles.summary:
Poll finds 66% of Americans think Trump is using position for monetary gain as his approval rating hits a new low

Most Americans think Donald Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself,…

blocks.text: Most Americans think Donald Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself, according to a new poll, as the US president’s approval rating falls to a new low ahead of November’s midterm elections.
A new Washington Post-ABC poll put Trump’s approval rating at 33% as he continues to crisscross the country as part of his campaign blitz for embattled Republicans.
Most Americans (66%) believe Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself, according to the survey – including 34% of Republicans. This is a 12-point jump from last September.

While Trump returned to power in January 2025 and promised a “new golden age” for the US economy, 48% of respondents said they are financially worse off than when Trump returned to office in 2025. According to the Post, this represents the highest percentage saying this about any president in this series of polls since 1986.

Most of those surveyed – 67% – also said Trump is not committed to protecting freedom of the press. This comes after a protracted battle to ban CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House grounds. A federal judge has subsequently issued a preliminary injunction blocking the administration from enforcing the ban.
Today’s new polling suggests Americans remain deeply pessimistic about the economy ahead of the midterms, with 75% rating conditions as either “not so good” or “poor”.
The findings also highlight the challenge facing Republicans in November: 37% of respondents said they trust Democrats more on the economy, compared with 28% who said they trust Republicans.

As Republicans across the country brace for a potentially tough set of results next month, 61% of Americans said Trump is not committed to free and fair elections, according to the poll. This number is up by five percentage points, compared to October 2025.

It also comes after the Department of Justice sued California, after the state did not supply the administration with the citizenship status of about 20,000 people it claimed to be non-citizens. However, the justice department did not provide an explanation for how they created the list of names.

articles.title: Journalists forced to flee homes after Tommy Robinson shared images of where they lived online, court told
articles.summary:
Far-right activist is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence to two MailOnline reporters

Journalists and their family members had to flee their homes after “bullyboy,…

blocks.text: Journalists and their family members had to flee their homes after “bullyboy, intimidatory tactics” were deployed by the far-right activist known as Tommy Robinson, a court has been told as his harassment trial got under way.

Robinson, 42, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, was alleged to have targeted journalists from the Daily Mail and Mail Online by circulating images of their homes to millions of online followers and in effect encouraging them to join in making threats.
He is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence to two MailOnline journalists, Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber in 2024, which Robinson denies.

Dirnhuber, a senior editor at the Mail, and his partner had to leave their home, while Young and his family were provided with a close protection officer after the alleged campaign of intimidation by Robinson.

Robinson, a former member of the British National Party (BNP) and co-founder of the English Defence League (EDL), is accused of harassment causing fear of violence through X posts and direct messages. He is also alleged to have made a telephone call on 5 August 2024 in which he is accused of telling Young he would visit his house, saying: “I’m coming to get you.”

Opening the case for the prosecution on Monday at Southwark Crown Court, barrister Ben Holt told the jury Robinson could have chosen to complain to a press regulator after the Mail reported on his alleged role as an “influencer” encouraging the violence that broke out after the Southport murders in July 2024.

The paper’s coverage included photos of Robinson reclining on a sunlounger, a phone in hand, while on holiday in Cyprus, where a team from the Daily Mail had located him. Members of the jury were shown an image of a front page which included a photo of Robinson and the headline: “Stoking Race Riots from his Sunbed.”
“This trial is about the defendant’s reaction to this, what he perceived to be, unnecessary intrusion into his holiday,” said Holt.

“On social media, to millions of followers, he circulated images of their homes. His supporters, followers, got involved, threatening the journalists. Understandably, you might agree, they were scared, in some circumstances being forced to leave their homes.

“That is what this trial is actually about. The prosecution say this defendant, using bullyboy, intimidatory tactics, threatened the journalists. He sent photographers to their home addresses. He put pictures, albeit redacted, of them out on his timeline on X for the enjoyment and appreciation of his followers.
Holt took the jury through Robinson’s reaction on X to the Mail’s coverage, which was said to have changed in tone from being “reasonable” and “concerned” to “retaliatory”.
Holt said that it was was inevitable “and would have been known” by Robinson that his online followers and supporters “would pick up the baton and attack” those he was talking about.

Examples given included tweets from an X account using the name The Secret SpAd, which posted the home address of Young while the journalist was still in Cyprus. It was posted with the comment: ”Please be sure to congratulate him.”

When Young returned home from Cyprus on 6 August, his wife and daughters told him that a man in a grey Audi had parked outside their home. The man was confronted by the journalist’s daughter but ignored her, and a report was made to police. A further report was made of a man sitting under a tree, pointing his camera at the house.
Holt told the court: “Mr Young was concerned. His main concern was that while (Robinson) himself might not harm him, one of his many supporters online may seek revenge on him or his family.”

The court heard that a third journalist who was involved the mail’s coverage, George Odling, also felt the need to leave his family home after becoming concerned with the publicity surrounding his colleagues.

Ted Verity, the editor-in-chief of the newspaper, provided evidence to police of a voicemail he received from an individual who identified himself as Tommy Robinson, who allegedly told him: “I’ve already located every fucking one of you.”
A video posted by Robinson’s X account was also played to the court, in which he accused the Mail of having “doxxed” his family and children.

In the video, he sad: “You broke up my family holiday. Is it fair that I do that to you? You know I know the locations to where you are. To any other journalist, I will find you. So please, think: is it right?”
The trial was adjourned until Tuesday morning.

articles.title: Ferocious criticism from all sides underlines Macron’s isolation
articles.summary: French president has compounded impression of arrogance with strategic errors – and consequences could be profound

blocks.text: The near-universal chorus of condemnation that greeted Emmanuel Macron’s address to the nation on Sunday, after one of the most violent days of rioting and looting in France’s recent history, was a stark reflection of just how weakened he now is.

Speaking from his office at the Élysée Palace, the president delivered an eight-minute speech expressing “anger and shame” after a weekend in which a town hall was set ablaze, 2,000-plus shops were looted, 2,300 people were arrested and 1,000 police injured.

A month-long protest by high school pupils over crumbling and crowded classrooms converged with broader frustrations over soaring living costs, rapidly widening inequality and falling public spending, bringing together students, teachers, trade unionists and a resurrected gilets jaunes movement.

Those largely peaceful protests were swiftly hijacked by masked groups who torched vehicles, ransacked businesses and severely damaged public infrastructure, including setting fire to Limoges’ city hall and invading that of Marseille.

Macron acknowledged the “deep anxiety” of young people but offered no concrete policy initiatives, no cabinet reshuffle and no new public spending, merely telling his prime minister to organise consultations and asking opposition politicians to take a stand.

The response, across the political spectrum, was damning. The Greens’ leader, Marine Tondelier, said that rather than “even beginning to make any kind of mea culpa”, Macron was “summoning us to the PM’s office like pupils to the blackboard”.

On the far right, the National Rally’s Jordan Bardella called the speech “lamentable” and said Macron had “nothing left to say” to the French. The party’s figurehead, Marine Le Pen, said the country was “caught in a vice between violence and impotence”.

The centre-right’s Bruno Retailleau said Macron was “totally overwhelmed”, while on the radical left, Jean-Luc Mélenchon accused the president of relying on “inaction and police brutality” in doomed hopes that the protests would simply fizzle out.

Perhaps most damagingly, even Macron’s former prime minister Édouard Philippe said he would have preferred “decisions and initiatives that might lead to a return to order and the restoration of state authority … Our country needs to be governed.”

Criticism is to be expected from rivals positioning themselves six months before a presidential election to choose Macron’s successor. But its sheer ferocity underlines his isolation, the disdain in which he is held, and the anger he inspires.

It is a structural trap that he has largely set for himself. Macron came to power in 2017 as a “Jupiterian” president – a deliberate strategy aimed at elevating the head of state above daily politics, projecting distant authority and technocratic brilliance.

But over nine years in the Élysée, that high-handed style – partly born, his critics say, of Macron’s complete lack of basic political experience as an elected official in a town hall or as a constituency MP – has morphed into perceived arrogance and detachment.

It has been compounded by catastrophic strategic errors, and France’s spiralling economic problems. Macron lost a functional parliamentary majority by refusing to meaningfully campaign between the presidential and legislative elections of 2022.

Two years later he dissolved the national assembly. That gamble backfired spectacularly, with voters returning an even more deadlocked parliament split between a divided left, a much-diminished centrist bloc and Le Pen’s far right.

Without a working majority, the government repeatedly resorted to controversial constitutional manoeuvres to force through laws without a parliamentary vote, laying it – and Macron – open to further accusations of democratic illegitimacy.

Compounding that institutional deadlock is a looming fiscal crisis. In decades gone by, French presidents facing mass protests on the streets could in effect buy a degree of social tranquility with targeted spending packages or public sector concessions.

But France’s national debt, at 119% of GDP, is at its highest level since 1946. Its budget deficit, at 5.1%, is also among the highest in the EU. There is just no money in the bank to ease the cost of living squeeze that brought 550,000 people on to the streets on Saturday.

The markets are worried: France’s borrowing costs are higher than Greece’s. And with few fiscal options, the government’s clearest response – in time-honoured French tradition – has been teargas and baton charges, sometimes against schoolchildren, further aggravating tensions.

The consequences for the presidential election could be profound. The centrist coalition built around Macron’s brand has all but collapsed. If the protests and violence persist, the main beneficiary will be the law-and-order champions of the far right.

Jean-Baptiste Moreau, an influential former MP from Macron’s party with whom the largely lame-duck president still occasionally speaks, reportedly went so far this weekend as to suggest he should resign and call early presidential elections.
“Macron still thinks he can change things,” he told Le Monde. “But at the moment, Marine Le Pen is on a direct path to the Élysée Palace.”

articles.title: Warning signs over threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car
articles.summary: The apparent attack on MP Helen Haines suggests the worst fears of politicians and public figures appear to have been realised.

blocks.text: As increasingly frequent acts of violence against politicians have shocked the globe in recent years, Australia has watched on with a contradictory feeling: that attacks like that could not happen here, and that it was only a matter of time until they did.

Australians will tell you this is a largely peaceful society with a comparatively civil public discourse. Violence targeting politicians has been rare, the bungled assassination of Labor leader Arthur Calwell in 1966 now a distant and fleeting memory.
But MPs and public figures – backed by experts – have been warning of a volcano of threats against them as social cohesion cracks, polarisation intensifies and the tone of debate grows hotter.
And on Monday, their worst fears appear to have been realised.
Independent MP Helen Haines was struck by a car and severely injured outside her office in the regional Victorian town of Wangaratta.
Police say a 43-year-old man was arrested at the scene, and a knife seized, but they have not said Haines was hit deliberately.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, however, swiftly described the incident as an apparent attack.

He was briefed by federal police – whose counter terror squad is helping state officers investigate – and told the national broadcaster: "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear."
Though he stressed no motive had been confirmed, Albanese earlier got emotional as he talked about the growing fear amongst MPs that they would end up targets.

Earlier this year Albanese himself was evacuated from his official residence over a bomb threat. As of August, about 20 cases in which people were accused of making violent threats against him were winding their way through courts around the country.

In recent years, politicians here have been mailed bullets. Female MPs – and in some cases their children – have been threatened with sexual violence. A Jewish MP's office has been firebombed, a Sydney mayor's car has been torched and countless other politicians have had their workplaces vandalised.

Just last week Small Business Minister Anne Aly said she had received a wave of death threats after a politician from the opposition said she should be "shamed and stoned in the square" over a tax policy.
According to government statistics, there were 1,067 reports of "harassing and threatening behaviour" against "high office holders" in the year to June: an increase on last year.
"We tend to bury our head in the sand and say, 'Not here', but this has been happening now for well over a decade," Josh Roose, a Deakin University Professor on violent extremism, tells the BBC.

Socioeconomic strain, growing mental health problems in the community, "grifters" who benefit politically or financially from whipping up further discontent, and a "carcinogenic" online environment are drivers of the trend, he says, which has dramatically escalated since the pandemic.
But the political class must also take responsibility for their role, he adds.

"We've seen a willingness to cross previously sacred terrain - you know, not targeting individuals, not targeting their families - but we now see that this is part and parcel of Australian political life.
"This is occurring at both ends of the political spectrum."
And experts like him warn it is not just politicians who are vulnerable: it is members of the media, academics, court officials and other public figures too.
Mike Burgess, the head of Australia's spy agency, has warned for years that the spectre of political violence is looming in Australia.

"Just as climate change increases the likelihood of extreme weather but does not forecast specific storms, politically motivated violence, including acts of terrorism, is more likely even though we cannot predict a specific attack," he said in his annual threat assessment for 2026.
And the Federal Police have said it is not just ideology motivating cases in recent times. "Grievance" is radicalising people.
"They're feeling distanced, they're feeling alone, they're looking for something to attach to, to give them meaning and purpose," Commissioner Krissy Barrett told the ABC earlier this month.

There have been frustrated rumblings in Canberra from some MPs who say security arrangements have not changed with the climate and – if a political motivation for this incident is confirmed – one of the greatest tenets of the nation's political culture could now be at risk.
It is not abnormal for you to run into your local member at the shops, or chat to them at the footy, and many open up their offices for constituents who want to raise concerns or share ideas.
Haines is particularly renowned and respected for that, Albanese said on Monday night.
"Here in Australia, it is a good thing that politicians are able to go about their community and engage with people," he said.

"I don't want to see a political system in which you can't have conversations with people at the supermarket, in the street, at street meetings, public forums – that's an important part of our democracy."

articles.title: New details emerge on two killed after woman drove through Kansas soccer game
articles.summary:
A boy, six, and woman, 35, were killed and 10 were injured after a woman drove on to the field at a youth soccer game

New details have emerged about two people – including a child – killed…

blocks.text: New details have emerged about two people – including a child – killed when a woman drove a vehicle through a youth soccer game in Kansas, as officials on Monday continued to investigate the cause of the tragedy.

Chris Adrian, a middle school soccer coach, said his family was heartbroken over losing his six-year-old son, Cole, who died after the incident at Wichita’s Stryker Sports Complex in which 10 others were hurt, some seriously.
“Cole was an incredible kid and could put a smile on anyone’s face,” Adrian said in a text message reported by the New York Times.
“He was the joy and light of our community. His pure heart was open to everyone. He had the best laugh. He was a friend with everyone, young or old.”
The other victim, 35-year-old Nicholas Schafer, was identified Sunday.

Schafer and his wife, Ashley, celebrated their 14th anniversary in May, according to a Facebook post, and had three children. An online fundraiser set up by friends said the family had “suffered tremendous loss, immense pain, and devastation, forever changing their futures”.
The two who died were unrelated and described as residents of McPherson, Kansas, about an hour north of Wichita.

A 34-year-old woman from Garden City, Kansas, who was at the wheel of the Chevrolet pickup truck at the center of the case, was released without charges by the Wichita police department on Sunday, pending further investigation and toxicology tests.
According to witnesses, the woman’s vehicle, also containing two of her three children, suddenly drove on to the field, having been parked in a space nearby.
Wichita’s police chief, Joe Sullivan, said in a statement on Facebook that his investigators “will continue working to understand exactly what happened”.

He said: “Our hearts are with the families of [Cole] and Nicholas as they face an unimaginable loss. What should have been a day of children playing soccer and families spending time together ended in tragedy.

“We are also thinking about those who were injured, their loved ones and everyone who witnessed what happened. We know this tragedy has affected many people throughout our community, and we want those families to know they are not alone.”
Those injured, Sullivan said, included five children: two girls ages five and nine, a five-year-old boy, and two boys aged eight.
Also injured were women aged 28, 59 and 65, and men aged 32 and 68. A 61-year-old woman was treated for medical complications unrelated to traumatic injuries.
Police said they have spoken to more than 30 witnesses so far and appealed for anybody with video of the incident to come forward.
Accounts of the tragedy were published on Monday by NBC News, which spoke to several people who were there.
Erica Case said she was watching her nine-year-old son’s game on an adjacent field when she heard an engine revving and several “boom” sounds.
“I saw the truck hitting things,” she said. “I saw debris flying in the air.
“I don’t know if it was a cone, a chair or a person, but you could see matter flying as the truck was barreling through the soccer field at a decent rate of speed.
“The moment that I recognized that that wasn’t gunshots, that that was bodies, I lost it, because it wasn’t just adults. It was also children.”
She said it took emergency services about 10 minutes to arrive, time in which bystanders raced to help those who were hurt. She said she saw one person giving CPR to one of the victims.
David Griekspoor was at the complex with his brother and sister-in-law, watching his nephew play soccer.
“It sounded like small gunfire – bap, bap, bap,” he told NBC. “You look up, and you just see the truck going through a line of people.”
The sports complex was closed for the remainder of the weekend after the incident.
On Sunday night, some members of the Wichita youth soccer community held a vigil and memorial at an indoor sports facility across town.

articles.title: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of planting device had Saudi support says court filing
articles.summary: The Saudi government did not immediately respond to BBC requests for comment.

blocks.text: A Saudi national charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's meeting rooms has been accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government, according to a court filing, external in California.

US prosecutors claimed Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked for the AI firm, was in "frequent communication... with a member of the Saudi royal family", and say a member of the country's military paid for a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia for his wife and son after his arrest.
It was argued the 35-year-old engineer therefore posed a flight risk and should be detained, pending trial.
The Saudi government did not immediately respond to BBC requests for comment.
Alfozan had worked at OpenAI for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant an audio recorder.
The AI company discovered the device, which was plugged into the back of a TV in a conference meeting room and covered up with toilet paper, on 30 September.
A camera was placed in the room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering and appearing to look behind the television where the audio recorder had been inserted.
He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI was terminated.

The court filing claimed the suspect's alleged conduct could pose "a danger to the national security of the United States", because executives from the tech firm met with government officials in the room during the days the device was believed to have been installed.
It said Alfozan's arrest came three days before he was scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way itinerary with his wife and son.

Following the arrest, the document claims the defendant's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her US visa was expiring" and so she and her son were "permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia", and her husband intended to do the same.

On 10 October, the day after Alfozan was arrested, his wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar. They travelled on a one-way business class ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official.
"Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through," the prosecutors argued.
The FBI investigation is ongoing.
Alfozan is scheduled to ‌appear ⁠in federal court in San Francisco later on Monday. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£188,000) fine.

articles.title: Masts removed from bomb-laden WWII ship in Thames in bid to avoid explosion
articles.summary:
American warship sank in 1944 with approximately 1,400 tonnes of munitions onboard

A sunken US wartime ship in the Thames estuary holding enough unexploded bombs to devastate a Kent coastal…

blocks.text: A sunken US wartime ship in the Thames estuary holding enough unexploded bombs to devastate a Kent coastal town and send a tidal wave through London has been made slightly safer, ministers have announced.

Engineers have removed the masts of the SS Richard Montgomery – a second world war cargo ship that sank in 1944 with approximately 1,400 tonnes of munitions onboard – without triggering the kind of feared explosion that has kept the wreck under constant guard for decades.
The work was carried out because of concerns that the masts, which had remained visible above the water near Sheerness, could collapse in on the deadly cargo and blow up the ship.

The potential effects of an explosion after 82 years under water have divided expert opinion. Some believe it could cause a small tsunami, throw debris 3km into the air, and “level Sheerness”, according to a New Scientist report in 2004. A government report in 2000 said it was widely accepted it would “put property and the local population at risk”.
The exact contents of the ship’s three holds are unknown but a defence agency report estimated there were almost 300 2,000lb (900kg) blockbuster bombs and more than 2,000 cluster bombs.

Keir Mather, the maritime minister, told the Commons on Monday that work had now been completed, with all three masts successfully removed in “complex project requiring specialist programme, engineering and risk management expertise”.
Mather said that the masts had put “significant load on the structure and their removal has reduced that risk and supports the long-term safe management of the site.”

blocks.caption: The masts have been taken to a maritime museum in Kent. Photograph: Fraser Gray/Shutterstock

blocks.text: He said work was completed ahead of schedule and below forecast costs, an estimated £9.5m. The masts have now been delivered to a maritime museum, the Historic Dockyard Chatham, “in recognition of the historic significance of the SS Richard Montgomery and its role in supporting the allied forces’ efforts during world war two”.
The wreck would “continue to be subject to continuous monitoring and control via the established exclusion zone”, he said.

A shipping exclusion zone has long been in place around the SS Montgomery, and since 2025 a no-fly zone has been in place – a development that could have been awkward had Boris Johnson’s proposed Thames estuary airport gone ahead.

Although the risk of an accidental major explosion is now deemed remote, local people have been alarmed by incidents in recent years, including the occasional close proximity of cargo shipping, and a paddleboarder who uploaded pictures to social media of himself leaning on the protruding masts.

articles.title: Houthi missile strike on Yemen camp kills 50 security recruits, local authorities say
articles.summary: Three missiles hit a camp in government-controlled Shabwa province that officials say was being used as a training centre for new recruits.

blocks.text: More than 50 security personnel have been killed and 200 injured in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa, local authorities say.

A spokesman for the Saudi-backed Yemeni armed forces said the Iran-backed group launched three ballistic missiles at al-Alam camp near Ataq city, which was being used as a training centre for recruits to the security forces and police.
The head of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, condemned what he called the "criminal attack" and promised a "firm response".
The Houthis' military spokesman said they had targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations".
Yemen's devastating civil war has flared up in recent months.
At the start of October, pro-government forces launched a major offensive that aims to retake territory in western Yemen that is controlled by the Houthis.

With air support from a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states, they managed to regain control of territory on the Red Sea coast that overlooks the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, which the Houthis captured in a surprise assault in September.
However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib and al-Jawf provinces.
The Houthis have also responded to the Saudi air strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in neighbouring Saudi Arabia.
Monday's attack in Shabwa is one of the deadliest reported since the start of the escalation.

Shabwa province's media office said in a statement that ballistic missiles struck the Martyr Ahmed al-Sulaimani Training Centre, where recruits from several provinces were undergoing training to be members of the internal security forces. According to a preliminary assessment, 53 were killed and more than 200 injured, it added.
A video posted on social media appeared to show several bodies scattered across the ground.

Shabwa's deputy governor, Fahad al-Khalifi, told AFP news agency that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to neighbouring Hadramout and Aden, where the government is based. Some of them were in a critical condition, he said.
Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said the attack constituted a war crime because the internal security forces training centre was not a military target.

He also accused the Houthis of "attempting to fabricate a false media victory, boost the morale of its collapsing elements, and cover up the defeats and setbacks it is suffering across various combat axes".
The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said in a statement that the missiles targeted a gathering of "Saudi enemy" forces at al-Alam camp, which he said was run by Saudi officers.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.

In a separate development, Houthi-run media reported that a Saudi air strike on a home in the Sahar district of the Houthi-controlled northern province of Saada on Sunday killed at least 10 people and injured 23 others, many of them women and children.
According to the Houthi-run health ministry in north-western Yemen, a total of 141 people had been killed in Saudi strikes over the past seven weeks.
The government's health ministry, meanwhile, said last week that at least 1,282 people had been killed in the conflict across Yemen since 6 August.
In Saudi Arabia, at least 19 people have been killed in Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom's airports since the beginning of October.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

articles.title: Obama blasts federal probe of congresswoman Ilhan Omar as 'so appalling'
articles.summary: Obama says federal agents' search of the Democrat's home was an effort to intimidate a Trump critic.

blocks.text: Barack Obama has said congresswoman Ilhan Omar is under federal criminal investigation simply because she's an outspoken critic of the President Donald Trump.

"The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president," the former US president wrote on X, calling the probe "so appalling".
The White House defended the inquiry, saying the justice department was "focused on restoring law and order".

Last week, homeland security agents searched the Minnesota Democrat's Washington DC home as part of an investigation into her immigration status. Born in Somalia, Omar moved to the US with her family as a child.
US media outlets have reported that the probe is tied to her American citizenship and whether she lied about her age when she arrived in the US in 1995.
Questions have been raised about whether the age listed on Omar's citizenship application differed from her actual birth date.
Obama said in his X post on Sunday that her father became a naturalised citizen when she was 17, and not yet legally an adult, which then gave her citizenship.

"Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen," he wrote.
"If this becomes the new normal," he added, "there's no reason to believe it will stop with her - or that future presidents, in either party, won't do the same."

According to the US Citizenship and Immigration Services, a child born outside of the US automatically becomes a citizen when he or she has at least one parent who is a citizen by birth or naturalisation, or he or she is under the age of 18, and is a lawful permanent resident living in the custody of a citizen parent.
White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis denied the investigation was politically motivated.
"Unlike Joe Biden, President Trump has not weaponized the Department of Justice against his political foes," she said in an emailed statement to the BBC.
"The Department is focused on restoring law and order and keeping Americans safe."
Trump has often argued that federal criminal investigations against him as he campaigned for re-election were politically motivated.

The investigation into Omar could lead to the justice department seeking to "denaturalise" her, or revoke her citizenship. It would have to prove there were material lies in the naturalisation process.
In 2023, Republicans removed Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee for comments and tweets she made about Israel, which drew bipartisan criticism.
Omar has said that Trump has targeted her for years with "baseless lies and smear campaigns" and called the investigation "the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation".
But Trump has said the investigation had "nothing to do" with him, while describing Omar as a "terrible person" and a "complainer".
Federal agents reportedly seized her phone, computers, notebooks and passport in the raid a week ago.

Her lawyers have demanded the government return her belongings, CBS News, the BBC's US partner, has reported, arguing in a letter sent on Friday that the seizure of property had violated restrictions put in place by a judge to protect her work as a federal lawmaker.

The lawyers also alleged agents did not duly notify Omar or the House of Representatives general counsel that a search would be taking place and kept her from contacting her attorney for more than an hour, according to CBS.

Democrats characterised the raid as the president attempting to interfere with the legislative branch of government. Republicans, meanwhile, have said Omar should be treated the same as anyone else under the law.

When Obama first ran for president, and throughout his two terms in the White House, Trump repeatedly raised questions about his citizenship, asserting he was not born on American soil and was disqualified from serving in office. Obama released two records proving he had been born in Hawaii.
Obama did not mention that history in his X post on Sunday.

articles.title: Farage claim that £5m was reward for Brexit was ‘not press office line’, close aide says
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Undercover footage of Dan Jukes raises fresh questions about Reform leader’s statement that £5m gift was for security

Nigel Farage undermined his own claims that a £5m gift was…

blocks.text: Nigel Farage undermined his own claims that a £5m gift was for security when he referred to the money as a reward for Brexit, according to one of his closest aides.
The apparent admission came in undercover footage seen by the Guardian in which Dan Jukes says that it is “priced in” for Farage to profit from politics.
The footage raises fresh questions about the party leader’s statements that the gift was solely for security purposes.

The Reform UK leader is awaiting the outcome of a parliamentary watchdog investigation into whether or not the £5m from the crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne, first revealed by the Guardian, should have been declared under parliamentary rules.

Farage told the Sun on 14 May: “And this [£5m] was given to me on an unconditional basis, completely unconditional basis. But frankly, it was given as a reward for campaigning for Brexit for 27 years.”

Now, previously unpublished footage from the undercover reporting group Verbatim, shared with the Guardian, has revealed a conversation between Jukes, a longtime close aide of Farage, and an undercover reporter.
“That was not the line to take from the press office,” Jukes said of Farage’s admission that the funds were a political reward, appearing to suggest that it was an on-air accident.

The subject of Farage’s funds arose when Jukes quipped that if a US limited liability company could not make a donation because of electoral law, perhaps the reporter posing as a donor could just make him a £5m unconditional gift instead.

After discussing if Jukes could think of any ways other than secret polling – foreign-funded polls that appeared to be orchestrated by Reform officials but which were not publicly attributed to the party – for the party to benefit from money from a US LLC, Jukes replied: “I’m happy to take a £5m personal, unconditional gift, of course.”
The undercover reporter said: “That seems like it’s [the £5m] been quite tough.”

“I’m a realist and I bat straight and it’s a little bit awkward,” Jukes said, appearing to admit that Farage was not meant to change his explanation from the £5m being intended for security costs to say it was a reward for Brexit.
“That was not the line to take from the press office,” Jukes said. “So I think now the line is it was a thank you for Brexit to pay for security so he is safe for the rest of his life.”
The undercover reporter suggested that people did not mind if Farage “makes a few bob [from politics]”.
Jukes replied: “Well it’s a bit priced in with our Nige, isn’t it, no one’s voting for him to be the pope.”

If the funds were not given unconditionally but rather as a way to circumvent donation rules, as the footage appears to suggest, it could also trigger questions about whether it was a payment for work and therefore subject to tax.
Jukes left Reform after the original Verbatim/Channel 4 investigation was aired. He had worked closely with Farage for more than a decade.
An internal Reform investigation concluded that neither Jukes nor another senior party official, James Orr, had broken laws that ban foreign donations. A police investigation is ongoing.

Harborne has previously said of the gift to Farage that it was “to support Nigel’s security not just now, but for the rest of his life”. Lawyers for the crypto-billionaire have previously said he “expected nothing in return” and “did not envisage Mr Farage returning to politics”.
The timeline for the gift is disputed.
Lawyers for Harborne have said the gift was made on 5 April 2024.
According to financial industry sources, some of the £5m was not received until the end of May, just before Farage announced on 3 June that he would stand as an MP.
The Guardian has also reported that Farage told senior Reform figures he would need “a million a year” to cover lost earnings if he stood for parliament in the 2024 general election.

Farage has given a wide variety of reasons for accepting the £5m including that it was for his security and a reward for Brexit. He has refused to say how much, if any, of the £5m has been spent on security, adding it was nobody’s business what he did with the money and he could “spend it on Ferraris” if he wanted.

A spokesperson for Farage did not address several of the points put to them by the Guardian, including the claim that Farage had deviated from the press office line by admitting the £5m was a reward for Brexit.
Farage’s spokesperson said Jukes “accurately describes that the gift was for his security for the rest of his life”.

Lawyers for Jukes referred back to a previous statement: “This was entrapment over a prolonged period of time by individuals, using selective editing, who had their own agenda to discredit Reform UK.”
They added that Jukes denied any wrongdoing and pointed to the outcome of Reform’s internal investigation.

articles.title: ‘Concerning issues’ found at GB power grid by inquiry into cover-up claims
articles.summary:
Neso control room staff accused senior executives of covering up extent of blackout risks during June heatwave

Independent investigators have found significant and concerning “cultural…

blocks.text: Independent investigators have found significant and concerning “cultural issues” at Great Britain’s grid operator after control room staff accused senior executives of covering up the extent of blackout risks in the UK during the June heatwave.

An external legal firm tasked with investigating a series of whistleblower allegations against the National Energy System Operator (Neso) raised concerns over how high levels stress among control room engineers was handled by the company.

The three-month investigation began after whistleblowers accused Neso of a cover-up over the growing risk of blackouts. They claimed the grid was becoming increasingly unmanageable, and that control room decisions were subject to “interference” by the company’s corporate affairs team to protect the reputation of the government-owned operator.
The unprecedented control room revolt included multiple internal complaints, the leak of internal documents to the press, and accusations of whistleblower intimidation.
Neso was forced to abandon plans for an internal investigation into the claims in favour of an independent investigation by the law firm Evershed Sutherlands, whose findings were published on Monday.

The law firm said that while it found “no evidence” of inappropriate influence over operational decisions, or that control room engineers were warned against leaving a paper trail of their efforts to stabilise the grid, the investigation found “cultural, governance and control issues” that were “significant findings in their own right”.

The allegations against Neso emerged after the June heatwave caused grid frequency levels to fall below normal operating limits on a number of occasions and required emergency assistance from neighbouring countries to keep the lights on.

The grid woes were caused by near-record temperatures that caused demand for electricity to run air-conditioning systems to surge while a high pressure heat dome slowed wind turbines and prompted unplanned outages at gas and nuclear plants across Europe.

Tim Jarvis, the chief executive of the regulator Ofgem, said that although the investigation did not uphold the whistleblower’s specific allegations, it raised “important and concerning issues about working culture and practices at Neso”.

The investigation found there were “high levels of stress and concern” within the control room over how staff would be able to keep the power system balanced as renewable energy replaces legacy fossil fuel power plants in line with the government’s net zero ambitions.

It said there was a view that senior Neso executives did not fully appreciate or understand the pressures faced by the control room engineers who were responsible for keeping the lights on “on the frontline”.

In addition, staff felt that their concerns or complaints went “largely unheard” because of the need to keep external stakeholders including the government and the regulators happy, according to the law firm’s report.
Fintan Slye, Neso’s chief executive, said the report was “constructive” in identifying areas in which the grid operator could improve how staff could raise concerns and how to respond to them.
after newsletter promotion
“I want all colleagues at Neso to feel heard. We will act on the recommendations, working closely with our trade unions, and be open with colleagues about the progress we make,” he said.

A separate Ofgem investigation, which is ongoing, will look into whether the cultural issues identified by Eversheds played a role in the operational decision-making, system security or raising energy costs for consumers.
“We will not prejudge that assessment,” Jarvis said, “But nor will we shy away from its conclusions. Our job is to establish the facts, identify the lessons and ensure action is taken.”

The Ofgem findings, which will be published no later than 31 March 2027, could lead to an enforcement investigation by the regulator if it believes Neso has not complied with obligations under market rules.
Michael Shanks, the minister for energy, said the government expected “significant action without delay” and would “keep progress under close review”.

articles.title: Kenyan starvation cult leader guilty of murder of 190 children and one adult
articles.summary:
Paul Mackenzie and his church set up sect that ordered followers to starve themselves and their children, say prosecutors

A Kenyan court on Monday found starvation cult leader Paul Mackenzie…

blocks.text: A Kenyan court has found the starvation cult leader Paul Mackenzie and about 30 others guilty of murder over the deaths of ⁠190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult-related disasters in recent history.
Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast ⁠in south-eastern Kenya.

Prosecutors say Mackenzie and ⁠his Good News International Church organised ​a Christian doomsday sect in which they ordered followers to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.
Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve but the ⁠court rejected that argument.
In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered from the Shakahola forest. Many were severely decomposed, and only 26 of them were able to be identified.
Monday’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into the other deaths are continuing.
Justice Diana Kavedza Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.

blocks.caption: Kenyan high court judge Diana Kavedza Mochache on 19 October. Photograph: EPA

blocks.text: Mackenzie was in ​court, wearing a striped polo shirt and red trousers, sitting alongside his wife, ‌one of the co-accused.
He was silent, ‌staring into space before the ruling was handed down.
Relatives of some of those who died in the forest gathered to hear the judgment at Mombasa high ‌court.
Francis Wanje, 62, lost eight family members including two grandchildren to the cult.

Speaking before the verdict, he said: “It has been really a heavy thing [for] us as a family, and it has really taken us very far in terms of psychological problems … I was hoping for this particular day.”
The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the coastal forest more than three years ago.

It raised questions over how Mackenzie was able to continue to operate despite having been on the radar of the authorities since 2017 when his premises were searched by police. In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.

blocks.caption: A Kenyan national youth service officer talks to a woman while on guard at the entrance to the Mombasa law courts on Monday 19 October. Photograph: Simon Maina/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.
Kenya’s president, William Ruto, said in 2023 that government agencies should have been ​able to prevent the deaths. He said he took responsibility as president.
People with direct knowledge of the cult’s activities said Mackenzie planned the mass starvation in three phases: first children, then women and young men, and finally the remaining men.

Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic, some of his followers told Reuters for a 2023 article.
Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene ⁠sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.

blocks.caption: Paul Mackenzie and his co-accused during their court appearance on 19 October. Photograph: Simon Maina/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The plight of his followers began ​to emerge in mid-March 2023, when a local man told ​police that his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.

Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives say he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police ​arrested him again in April 2023 and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.
Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths including terrorism-related ones, which he has denied.
Prosecutors say while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles (30km) from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

articles.title: Supreme court rejects effort to revive plea deal for Khalid Sheikh Mohammed in 9/11 attacks
articles.summary:
Agreement would have spared Mohammed risk of execution in exchange for guilty plea and life in prison

The supreme court on Monday rejected an effort to revive a plea deal for Khalid Sheikh…

blocks.text: The supreme court on Monday rejected an effort to revive a plea deal for Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind of the attacks on 11 September 2001.
The agreement would have spared Mohammed the risk of execution in exchange for his guilty plea and a sentence of life in prison without parole.

Mohammed is accused of developing and directing the plot to crash hijacked airliners into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon 25 years ago. Another of the hijacked planes crashed into a field in Pennsylvania.
The plea agreement was approved by military prosecutors and the Pentagon’s senior official for Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, before Lloyd Austin, then the defense secretary, stepped in.
Austin threw out the deal in 2024, saying a decision on the death penalty in an attack as grave as September 11 should only be made by the defense secretary.

Relatives of the September 11 victims were split on the agreements for Mohammed and two co-defendants. Some said a trial was the best path to justice, while others saw it as the best hope for bringing the long, painful case to a conclusion.
Defense attorneys had argued that Austin, who served under Joe Biden, acted too late. But a divided appeals court panel found Austin acted within his authority.
A trial date has been set for 2028.

articles.title: Kenya: Cult leader guilty of murdering 190 children, 1 adult
articles.summary: Preacher Paul Mackenzie was accused of encouraging his followers to starve themselves to death. He ran a Christian doomsday cult called the Good News International Church that claimed the end of the…

image.caption: Paul Mackenzie arrived at court under police escort ahead of the verdictImage: Laban Walloga/REUTERS

blocks.text: A court in Mombasa, Kenya, on Monday found self-proclaimed preacher Paul Mackenzie and 28 associates guilty of murdering 190 children and one adult as part of a notorious Christian starvation cult.
Mackenzie established his so-called Good News International Church in 2003 and was alleged to have incited his followers to starve themselves to death in order to "meet Jesus."
He was arrested in April 2023 after a rights group informed authorities.
Some of his acolytes were rescued but the subsequent police operation exposed hundreds of mass graves at a forest site near the Kenyan beach resort of Malindi.
Local media dubbed the case the "Shakahola Forest Massacre."
Shakahola Forest Massacre: What did the judge say?

"I am satisfied that the prosecution has proved the case against all the 29 accused persons for the murder of 190 children and one adult," said Justice Diana Kavedza Mochache after a hearing which lasted over eight hours.

blocks.caption: Justice Diana Kavedza Mochache delivered the verdict Image: Laban Walloga/REUTERS

blocks.text: The prosecution had said Mackenzie "initiated and directed" extreme fasting at his 800-acre (325 hectare) ranch in Shakahola Forest, claiming there was a "structured hierarchy of death" which said children should die first, followed by teenagers, women, and then men.
Post-mortems and police reports revealed that the children mostly died from starvation, but also from "asphyxia, neck compression and traumatic head injury," prosecutors said.
The court in Mombasa also heard that, in some cases, children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.
"This is a very, very important day," said Francis Wanje, 62, who lost eight family members, including his daughter and two grandchildren, at Shakahola.

"We are expecting a ruling that will be a lesson to the whole public, so that such kinds of things will not happen again," he told the AFP news agency, expressing anger over the government's initial inaction.
Will Kenya's cult leader be found guilty of manslaughter?
Mackenzie facing even more Shakahola charges

Since the initial discovery of the graves, even more bodies of children, women and men have been unearthed, bringing the total to well over 400. The soaring death toll has even required sporadic pauses in excavations as local morgues ran out of space.
In January 2026, Mackenzie was charged over a further 52 bodies found at a nearby village.
There have been calls in Kenya for tougher regulations on religious organizations after it emerged that Mackenzie had been arrested twice in the past but released.
He was arrested in 2017 on charges of "radicalization" but was acquitted. He was arrested again in 2019 in relation to two child deaths at Shakahola, but released on bail.
His sentencing will take place on November 6.
How do radical churches get people to follow their beliefs?

articles.title: Houthi attack kills 53 in biggest single loss of life since Yemen civil war reignited
articles.summary:
More than 200 mostly young people said to be injured after ballistic missile attack on training camp for government forces

At least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile…

blocks.text: At least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government forces, making it the largest single loss of life since the country’s civil war reignited in September.

The attack on al-Alam camp in the southern Shabwa province was said to have injured more than 200 others, mostly young recruits, and described as a disaster by the country’s UN-recognised government. The injured were taken from the police and army training camp in the Jardan district to a hospital in the local capital, Ataq, where pleas for blood donations were made.

There will be an inquiry into how so many troops were left so exposed to a Houthi attacks. In mid-September, the group began a fresh push on forces backing the UN-recognised government by pushing south along the Red Sea coast to try to take control of the Bab al-Mandab waterway.

Reliable assessments of the death toll in the fighting over the last month are hard to gather, but it is running into the many thousands. A Saudi airstrike on Sunday killed nine, including five children and two women.

Rashad al-Alimi, the president of the UN-recognised government, said those killed on Monday were new recruits, and he vowed an immediate hard response. He said the incident “affirmed that targeting the recruits reflects the Houthi militias’ approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter”.
He had already on Monday phoned the UN secretary general, António Guterres, to ask for the UN to classify the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation.

The Shabwa provincial authority said: “Targeting recruits constitutes a military escalation and a blatant assault on the province’s security.” Its governor, Awad bin Al-Wazir, visited the wounded in hospitals.

The killings underline the dangers of large numbers of troops gathering in one place within reach of the Houthi ballistic missile arsenal. The training camp was struck by three ballistic missiles while the recruits lined up in formation.
Houthi forces have also cut the road between government-run Shabwa and the Houthi-run Bayda governorate.

The Houthi military spokesperson said: “Our armed forces targeted the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations in the Al-Alam camp, which is run by Saudi officers in the eastern regions. The targeting resulted in the fall of dozens of dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilizations, including Saudi officers.

“We warn the deceived ones against responding to the Saudi enemy’s calls to lure them with his defiled money to the pyres of death, and to exploit them instead of his soldiers who are indifferent to their lives.”
Fighting is also under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of the Yemeni city Taiz, and citizens have been calling for greater air protection.
Southern forces were said to be making progress in edging Houthi forces out of control of the area around the Bab al-Mandab, the narrowest waterway taking ships from the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
It is not clear whether the Houthis have decided to slow the pace of attacks on Saudi airports and energy installations, or they are running low on munitions.

The Saudi Armaco headquarters was struck last weekend and some airlines have said they are not yet going to resume using Riyadh airport. The airport formally reopened at the weekend after being attacked this month.
Hans Grundberg, the UN envoy for Yemen, is due in London to meet ministers on Tuesday.

articles.title: In pictures: French landmarks damaged and destroyed by violent protesters
articles.summary: France is used to protests but the violence and damage seen across the country is shocking many people.

blocks.text: ByPaulin Kola and Pilar TomásVisual journalist
Local curfews may come into force in French towns following a weekend of disorder.
Most of the protesters were peaceful in expressing their opposition to rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.
But others - dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas - set fire to cars, shops and buildings.
The scale of the destruction - including to some iconic landmarks - has shocked many in a country used to street protests.
The damage in the capital city is extensive. Shop fronts have been broken and stores looted.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Kiosks, vehicles and buildings were set alight and destroyed close to some of the city's most recognisable areas, including here at Place De La Republique in Paris

blocks.text: Image source, PA Media
Kiosks, vehicles and buildings were set alight and destroyed close to some of the city's most recognisable areas, including here at Place De La Republique in Paris

blocks.caption: Image caption, Front doors and windows were broken down as looting broken out in several cities

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Front doors and windows were broken down as looting broken out in several cities

blocks.caption: Image caption, Some groups erected barricades on the Champs-Elysees in Paris

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Some groups erected barricades on the Champs-Elysees in Paris
The iconic Place de la Republique was vandalised, too.
A yellow vest - representative of the movement which helped co-ordinate the weekend protests - was draped around the body of the Statue of the Republic, erected in 1883.
Groups of rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, took over parts of the capital and wreaked havoc.
Tear gas and stun grenades were fired at hundreds of people but police struggled to contain smaller groups of people roving around the city attack businesses.
The full extent of the damage did not become clear until dawn broke on Sunday.

blocks.caption: Image caption, This bakery was one of several businesses set on fire in Paris

blocks.text: This bakery was one of several businesses set on fire in Paris

blocks.caption: Image caption, Some groups piled rental bikes in the middle of roads and set them alight

blocks.text: Some groups piled rental bikes in the middle of roads and set them alight

blocks.caption: Image caption, Cars were set alight close to the Porte Saint-Denis in the capital

blocks.text: Cars were set alight close to the Porte Saint-Denis in the capital
Further south in Marseille, protesters broke into the city hall by using a metal fence as a battering ram.
A bust of Marianne - symbol of the French Republic - was damaged and knocked to the floor in Marseille as people ransacked the building.

blocks.caption: The statue of Marianne, damaged when protesters vandalised the lobby of Marseille's city hall, is seen on the floor inside the building

blocks.text: City Mayor Benoît Payan was furious with the "almost total lack of control" by the security forces.
"The world's sixth largest power does not deserve this. The world is watching us, this morning we are the shame of Europe," he said.
In the city of Lyon, Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office, housed in a 19th Century building, was "a tragedy".
Chaos around the tourist office in Lyon as flames engulf it
Fire crews also battled a fire at Limoges town hall, which caused part of the building to collapse. Local officials said the town hall was "largely lost".
"A wild horde" had "deliberately" set fire to the 143-year-old building, said Maurice Barate, the prefect for the Haute-Vienne department.

blocks.caption: Image caption, In Limoges, the spire at the top of the ornate city hall has been destroyed by the fire

blocks.text: In Limoges, the spire at the top of the ornate city hall has been destroyed by the fire
French authorities have admitted they lost control of cities to the protesters.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez offered his resignation - which has been rejected.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has given local mayors the power to introduce partial curfews in some parts of the country, which he says is designed to protect people and businesses.
But the French are holding their breath - in anticipation of another chapter in this protest next Saturday.

articles.title: Canada: Alberta votes on holding independence referendum
articles.summary: Canada's oil-rich western province of Alberta is not deemed likely to vote in favor of a real breakaway plebiscite. Nevertheless the separatist movement hopes to gain leverage over Mark Carney's…

image.caption: Alberta is a vast, resource, rich state with a population slightly smaller than Finland or New ZealandImage: Jeff McIntosh/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Residents of Alberta in Canada are voting in a referendum on whether the province should begin a process that could ultimately lead to independence.
The motion does not appear likely to succeed but the vote taking place at all signifies economic and political grievances gaining some sway in the vast oil-rich region.
Separatist leaders hope that a comparatively strong showing for their cause could nevertheless pressure Prime Minister Mark Carney's government in Ottawa to pay them more heed in future.
What will happen during the vote?
Polls opened at 9 a.m. local time in the provincial capital Edmonton (1500 GMT/UTC) on Monday.
They are scheduled to close at 8 p.m. that evening (Tuesday, 0200 GMT/UTC).
Results will then be published as they come in.
At least based on opinion polls, the yes/no result is in no real doubt, but as many as 1 in 3 voters might support the proposal.

blocks.caption: The 'no to the nine' campaign urges voters to refuse all nine proposal up for debate, not just the most significant one on setting the wheels in motion for a potential independence referendumImage: Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What has led to the vote?

Monday's referendum is the first on the notion of breaking away from Canada in a province other than majority French-speaking Quebec, which has a better-known separatist movement founded in language and cultural differences.

The vast oil-rich state is almost double the size of Germany in terms of land mass, but is much more sparsely populated with around 5 million residents. Almost half of them live in its two main cities, Edmonton and Calgary.
Alberta's provincial government is led by Danielle Smith of the United Conservative Party while Mark Carney's Liberal Party lead the national government.

Smith herself does not advocate independence and has urged voters to oppose the motion. But she has nevertheless authorized the vote, seemingly in a bid to assuage an increasingly vocal flank within her own ranks.

Independence advocates accuse the government of stifling Alberta's oil industry, for instance through environmental regulations, and also say they contribute disproportionately to the national public purse.

"Canada has an imbalanced system which feeds the central population and government at the expense of the outlying producing provinces such as Alberta," said Cory Morgan, founder of a pro-separation organization called Pathway to Independence.

blocks.caption: PM Carney has been campaigning in Edmonton and elsewhere, trying to maximize turnout among those who favor staying part of CanadaImage: John Ulan/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Canadian sovereignty under pressure from within and without

Carney, who grew up in Alberta, has spent much of the past week campaigning for the "stay" campaign, appealing to national pride and urging supporters to vote to provide as resounding a result as possible — even in what might not be a close race.
The renowned economist and central banker often argued that the separatist cause might be guilty of overlooking matters more significant than dollars and drilling permits.
"Canada is not a transaction between provinces. It's not about gross and net, gives and gets," he said at an event in Red Deer on Friday.

Although polls in French-speaking Quebec suggest that enthusiasm for independence — typically a minority cause — is lower than usual during Carney's premiership, the issue is never very far from the political debate. The success of the separatist Parti Quebecois in local elections this month served as a reminder of this.
Carney is also trying to maintain national unity amid pressure from Canada's nearest neighbor and biggest trade partner.
US President Donald Trump is conducting characteristically combative trade talks with Canada that have seemed in danger of breaking down in recent months.
When at his most agitated, Trump has even called for Canada to become the "51st state" of the US. He has also tried to rename bodies of water like Lake Ontario.
Why Canada's trust in the US may not recover anytime soon

articles.title: Can diplomacy prevent an Ethiopia-Eritrea war as Tigray gets a new administration?
articles.summary: Ethiopia has installed a new administration in conflict-hit Tigray after federal forces pushed back Tigrayan fighters. But tensions with Eritrea continue to raise fears of a wider regional war.

image.caption: Ethiopia has installed an interim administration in Tigray tasked with holding elections and rehousing displaced peopleImage: Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed on Friday announced an interim government in the country's northern Tigray region and gave it six months to prepare for regional elections and restore stability.

Abiy's announcement followed a military offensive launched in September by the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and six other armed groups. They were ultimately forced to retreat and lost control of the region.

"To attain the peace that has long eluded them, to secure their right to self-administration, ​and to finally enjoy the fruits of development — which have been out of reach for many years — the people of Tigray must break free from this cycle ⁠of conflict," ​Abiy said in a statement posted on X.

Shishay Amare, the new mayor of the regional capital Mekelle, said: "Our role is to create the right conditions for elections by ensuring peace and stability across Tigray," reported French news agency Agence France-Presse (AFP).

"I am confident that this will be done within six months, according to our plan," Amare said, adding that their priorities included restoring peace, helping displaced residents return home, reopening markets and ensuring humanitarian assistance reached those in need.
Why relations with Eritrea matter

The fighting has revived concerns about a return to the devastating 2020–2022 Tigray war. Around 1 million people remain displaced from that conflict. The African Union has estimated that the war resulted in around 600,000 deaths from combat, famine and the collapse of healthcare.
The new administration faces unresolved disputes over political authority and territory, including western Tigray, which is claimed by both Tigray and neighboring Amhara state.

blocks.caption: Egypt and Ethiopia have repeatedly clashed over the construction of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD)Image: Brian Inganga/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ethiopia and Eritrea were once bitter enemies but signed a peace agreement in 2018. Eritrean forces later fought alongside Ethiopian federal troops during the Tigray war. The countries' relationship has since deteriorated.
Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of supporting Tigrayan forces and violating Ethiopian territory. Eritrea has denied the accusations.
Reports of Eritrean troop movements near the border have heightened concern, although the extent of any current deployment remains disputed.

Tsedale Lemma, journalist and publisher of the prominent Addis Standard magazine, told DW earlier this month that the danger reflects years of unresolved tensions and failures to implement the November 2022 Pretoria Agreement, which ended the previous Tigray war.

Asked whether the international community was underestimating the threat, Lemma said: "It is absolutely underestimating it." She argued that international actors had failed to ensure effective monitoring of the agreement and respond adequately as the peace process weakened.
A wider regional risk
The confrontation comes amid instability across the Horn of Africa, including Sudan's war and tensions between Ethiopia and Egypt over the Nile mega-dam project.
Why northern Ethiopia is seeing growing violence once again
Last year, Ethiopia inaugurated the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), a move that was not well received by neighboring Egypt and Sudan, both downstream countries.
Competition over access to the Red Sea adds another strategic dimension: Ethiopia became landlocked when Eritrea gained independence in 1993.

Journalist Martin Plaut, who specializes in the Horn of Africa, has warned that the region faces a crossroads. He has raised the possibility of Ethiopian forces entering Eritrea, but an invasion remains a scenario, not a confirmed decision by the Ethiopian government.

Any wider conflict could threaten regional trade and maritime security. The Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait connect shipping routes between Europe and Asia, making the region strategically important well beyond Africa.
Can diplomacy avert war between Ethiopia and Eritrea?
The United States and the United Kingdom have called on Ethiopia and Eritrea to exercise restraint and return to dialogue under their 2018 peace framework.
Speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews on Saturday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned that the military buildup on the Ethiopia-Eritrea border could escalate into a wider conflict.
Rubio said Washington hoped lifting some sanctions would improve communication with both sides and stressed the need for a "wise and measured" response to avoid a broader regional war.

A UK government spokesperson said in an October 15 statement that: "We urgently call for de-escalation and a return to dialogue. We reiterate our support for the African Union's role in facilitating this."
For now, the recapture of towns in Tigray has changed the military balance but has not resolved the tensions surrounding the region.
Whether international pressure can prevent a wider war will depend on whether the governments involved choose dialogue over further escalation.
Negash Mohammed, Tamirat Geleta and Christine Mhundwa contributed to this report.

articles.summary: The workers are stationed at factories in Windsor and Toronto — as well as the idled Brampton assembly plant.

image.caption: Workers leave the Stellantis Windsor Assembly Plant earlier this year. (Michael Evans/CBC)

blocks.text: Windsor·Breaking
The workers are stationed at factories in Windsor and Toronto — as well as the idled Brampton assembly plant.
Employees stationed in Windsor, Toronto — as well as idled Brampton assembly plant
Stellantis workers represented by Unifor have voted 97 per cent in favour of a strike mandate as collective bargaining negotiations remain stalled.
Two days of voting were held on the weekend.

items: Unifor to hold strike authorization votes at Stellantis

blocks.text: Unifor has said any potential strike action remains its last resort.

“When you deliver a strike authorization vote north of 97% across our Stellantis workplaces, you send a powerful message of unity and strength," said James Stewart, Unifor Local 444 President, in a social media video released Monday morning.
"You have given us the tools to get this done.”
A key sticking point has been the uncertainty around the Brampton factory. Recently, Stellantis said it planned to sell the property to defence contractor Roshel.
More than 2,000 workers were laid off in Brampton in 2023, and the automaker later moved production of its Jeep Compass to Illinois.

items: Stellantis says tariffs, consumer demand driving weeks-long layoffs at Windsor plant

blocks.text: Unifor has argued that closing and selling Brampton would threaten workers' wages, pensions and benefits, and have broader consequences for Ontario's automotive sector and supply chain.
Stellantis Canada president and CEO Trevor Longley has earlier said the company considers Canada an important market and has invested more than $8 billion across its Canadian operations since 2022.
In Windsor, a third shift was restored in February of this year.
More to come.
