articles.title: Myanmar refugees find hope in Thailand's work program
articles.summary: A year ago, Thailand granted long-staying refugees from Myanmar the right to work legally. Refugees and rights groups welcome the move but say the program's first year has exposed significant…

image.caption: Thailand's work program has allowed thousands of Myanmar refugees living in camps to support themselves and their families [FILE: May 28, 2024]Image: Matt Hunt/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: At a glance, Ray Boe doesn't stand out from the tens of thousands of other foreign workers toiling at countless construction sites that push Bangkok's soaring skyline ever higher.
Unlike most of them, though, the 31-year-old came to Thailand's capital from one of the country's nine camps for refugees who have fled decades of civil strife inMyanmar.
The camps, which hug the Thai-Myanmar border, are home to more than 100,000 people — in some cases since the 1980s, when the refugees first started arriving.
Until a year ago this month, the Thai government had refused to let them leave the camps to find work, forcing most to live hand-to-mouth on foreign donor aid.
That changed in October 2025, after foreign aid cutbacks — mostly by the United States — forced the camps to slash the food support and healthcare they could provide.
New Thai labor scheme offers hope for Myanmar refugees
Around the same time, fighting between Thailand and Cambodia over territorial claims had sent hundreds of thousands of migrant workers from Cambodia back home, leaving behind a yawning labor gap.
Myanmar refugees allowed to work outside of camps
To cope with the aid cuts and labor deficit, the Thai government reversed decades of policy and began issuing the refugees permits to work outside the camps, to help them meet their own needs.
Ray Boe is one of the 6,800 camp refugees the government said have entered the Thai labor force in the first year of the program.
"After the cuts by USAID and other organizations, there is no more regular support for our daily needs, like rice and other rations. And there is not enough healthcare in the camps anymore," he said.
The cuts forced him and his parents to borrow from neighbors and to pare down their already modest meals.
Underpaid and overworked: Myanmar migrants in Thailand

Since last month, he has earned 400 baht (about $12) a day pouring concrete and erecting scaffolding around what's to be a 12-story apartment building in central Bangkok. He hopes to start sending money home soon.
"It will help us pay for food and other basic needs, and for health are for my parents," Ray Boe said.

"Compared to how we were living in the camp before, it will be a big difference, having my own income and supporting my family on my own, not having to wait for other people to support us day to day," he told DW.
Refugee work program offers hope, but faces a rocky start
The program allows the refugees to work in 43 of Thailand's 76 provinces and in any sector not reserved by law for Thai citizens only.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said the government has improved the vocational training on offer inside the camps to better prepare refugees for work outside.

"We are hopeful that this policy would enhance opportunities and empower the [refugees] to realize their potential, as well as contribute to Thai socioeconomic development," said Praporn Waenluang, a spokesman for the ministry's information department.
Labor and refugee rights groups have welcomed the program.

"I have met a lot of camp [refugees] who have come outside and worked. They are so happy to work and earn money, a lot of money compared to what they [can] get in the camp," said Siwawong Sooktawee, Thailand project coordinator for the International Detention Coalition.
"This is good because they feel they can help themselves, they can support themselves, not depend on aid anymore," he added.
Myanmar workers in Thailand struggle to work legally
Yet he and others have said the program has gotten off to a slow start, with many flaws to work out.

They said many of the refugees who have taken part have not been given contracts by their employers, only to find the conditions rougher, the work harder, or the pay lower than what they were promised before leaving the camps. The program also lacks a clear system for lodging and settling complaints, according to observers.

"Many refugees go, come back, go, come back so many times. Some refugees, their families have to raise funds or borrow money in the refugee camps so that their father or their family member will be able to return," said K'nyaw Paw, general secretary of the Karen Women's Organization, an NGO serving the camp's ethnic Karen group.
Financial burdens placed on Myanmar refugees

Siwawong and K'nyaw Paw said refugees are sometimes made to repay employers through wage deductions for hiring them, including medical exams, government permits and transportation to job sites. As a result, they often start work already in debt, sometimes without prior warning.

Akwah, a father of two who goes by one name, left his camp with 20 other refugees in November 2025 for what was supposed to be a job harvesting sugarcane on a farm on the other side of the country for 250 baht per day.

When he arrived, however, he was told to cut eucalyptus trees — a much more difficult and dangerous job, he said — for only 200 baht per day. Workers had to sleep outdoors, with no electricity and only a nearby pond for water.
"We spoke to the boss, but the boss did not care. He said, 'Just do the work because you are already here.' But we said we could not do it," said Akwah. They left after three months.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not reply to DW's request for comment on the program's alleged problems. The Labor and Interior ministries, which mainly oversee the program, did not reply to requests for an interview either.
Rights groups say program still needs to improve

Siwawong and K'nyaw Paw said refugees who take part should be guaranteed clear and detailed contracts — translated if needed into Burmese, Karen or Karenni, the main languages spoken in the camps — and an easy-to-access system for filing and settling complaints.
They also suggest that the government open more provinces up to the program and screen the job brokers coming to the camps as middlemen, to weed out the unscrupulous ones.

They said their NGOs and others are working with the government on making some of the upgrades, and that they're hopeful the program will improve with time, so that more of the refugees are able and willing to take part.
The Thailand-Myanmar border clinic for people fleeing war
For all the program's flaws, though, they said most of the refugees are still eager to apply, even those who have run into problems.

"I had a bad experience, but I still want to go again, because food in the camp is a problem," said Mu Dah Hsit, who fell ill at her job and had to quit after her boss refused to cover the health insurance the program is supposed to guarantee.
"I have no mother, and a father who is sick, and siblings I have to take care of," she said. "So, I have to go; otherwise, we cannot live."

articles.title: Rubio visits India with a trip to the world's largest oil refinery topping the agenda
articles.summary: A visit to India this week by Washington's top diplomat will skip New Delhi and instead include the world's largest oil refinery, which processes massive amounts of Russian crude. Is Trump looking…

image.caption: Ahead of his arrival in India, Rubio said a trade deal was 'close' Image: Kylie Cooper/REUTERS

blocks.text: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio kicks off a three-day visit to India on Monday in the finance hub of Mumbai, before heading to Jamnagar, home to a major oil refinery owned by industrial titan Reliance Industries.
Rubio's business-oriented visit comes as trade talks remain stalled amid continued ambiguity on punitive measures from the US over India's purchases of Russian oil.

Reliance is a top buyer of Venezuelan oil. The refinery can process 1.4 million barrels of crude oil a day, so it's a valuable exporter of diesel fuel for global markets. The refinery has also been a major buyer of Russian Urals crude, making it a significant part of India's energy relationship with Russia.
In March, Washington unveiled plans for a new oil refinery in Texas, backed by Reliance.

US President Donald Trump has put the value of the project at $300 billion (€258 billion) and presented it as a way to help reduce the US trade deficit with India. Whether the project moves forward, and on what terms, will be closely watched.
An elusive US-India trade deal

Since taking office for a second time in 2025, Trump has gone back and forth on tariff threats with India over what he considers to be unfair trade practices, along with India's continued purchases of Russian oil amid the war in Ukraine.
How India has become Russia's trade lifeline

In February 2026, Trump announced a "trade deal" that slashed US tariffs on Indian goods, in exchange for India lowering trade barriers and halting purchases of Russian oil. Trump had claimed that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi promised to stop buying Russian oil. However, this has never been confirmed by New Delhi.

While maritime data from Kpler, a commodities and energy-market intelligence company, showed Indian refiners briefly diversified supply away from Russia to avoid tightening sanctions, India's deep reliance on discounted Russian crude continues to be a cornerstone of its energy strategy. Russia remains India's top supplier of crude oil.
In mid-September, Trump signed the "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act," imposing 100% tariffs on top buyers of Russian oil and gas, which includes India.
However, last week, just days before the legislation was due to go into effect, Trump signed an executive order pausing the sanctions.
Rubio: Trade deal 'very close'

Before traveling to India, Rubio was in Uzbekistan for a meeting of the "C5+1" diplomatic platform comprising the US and five Central Asian countries. In remarks on the sidelines, Rubio said trade talks with India are taking place with the sanctions waivers in mind.

blocks.caption: Jamnagar is the largest single-site oil refinery in the worldImage: Reliance Industries Limited/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "We have had to waive sanctions over the past few months, looking at the global supplies, looking at global prices, and the impact it was having on other countries," he said.
"We're trying to finalize a trade deal with India right now. We're very close to doing that," Rubio added.
In an interview with Indian broadcaster NDTV, US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said that Jamnagar could be a valuable source of diesel for the US.

Foreign policy analyst C Raja Mohan of Jindal Global University in India told DW that Rubio skipping a visit to the Indian capital in favor of Mumbai and Jamnagar should not be considered a diplomatic snub, as the refinery has international importance amid the global energy crunch brought on by the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East.
He said Jamnagar is an "important node in global trade" because it processes Russian oil and serves as a conduit for refined Russian petroleum products reaching Western markets.

Although Trump's sanctions reprieve offers New Delhi temporary relief, the underlying threat remains. Washington retains the option of imposing punitive tariffs, leaving Russian oil as a potential source of leverage in wider trade negotiations.
Former Indian ambassador to the US, Meera Shankar, cautioned against reading too much into Rubio's decision to skip Delhi amid political criticism in India.

"The focus of his current trip is on energy, and he is visiting the Reliance refinery in Jamnagar," she told DW. "The high price of fuel, particularly diesel, has become a political liability for the Trump administration, which wants to be seen taking action on this issue."

Diesel prices have skyrocketed around the world following the Iran war and the ensuing disruption of supply from the Middle East. In waiving Russia sanctions, Trump has tried to blame Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil facilities as being the cause of high prices.
Shankar pointed to Reliance's proposed Texas refinery, noting that the state is "one of the states in play" in the upcoming midterm elections in the US.
"Some forward movement on the investment would be welcome," she said.
Can Trump’s diesel deal bring down US fuel prices?
Trump eroding trust in Delhi?
The two governments continue to describe their ties as a comprehensive global strategic partnership spanning defence, trade, technology and energy.
Analyst Mohan argued that describing the US-India relationship as uniquely transactional was misleading.
"Every nation ultimately acts out of national self-interest, rather than pure altruism or shared values," he said.
The current friction, in his view, is part of a normal negotiation between two sovereign powers, not proof that the partnership was failing.
Besides Russian oil, another potential area of complication is the Trump administration suspending a scheme allowing US companies to sponsor skilled foreign workers.

On October 8, the Trump administration suspended new and pending applications under the US Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) program at several technology companies amid investigations into alleged visa fraud and the displacement of US workers.
The process is a key step for employers seeking permanent residency for foreign staff, including Indian professionals.

Harsh Pant, vice president for studies and foreign policy at the Delhi-based Observer Research Foundation (ORF), said Trump's own words and actions had damaged ties despite regular high-level engagement.
"Even as he calls Prime Minister Modi a good friend, he has damaged the relationship by targeting India, and his supporters have been targeting Indians," Pant told DW.
Pant said inconsistent messaging from Washington was eroding trust and could have consequences well beyond Trump's presidency.
"The sense that America is unreliable, that America can't be trusted, is beginning to come back into policy discourse," he said.

The damage, he warned, could reach beyond government-to-government relations to Indian students, professionals and the middle class, whose goodwill has helped sustain ties through earlier disagreements.

"If public sentiment goes against a country, then it becomes very difficult for the policy-makers to craft an alternative policy,” Pant said, adding that US actions affecting Indian students and professionals "will have consequences."
India: From tariff fortress to free-trade powerhouse

articles.title: League-leading NU wants to prove doubters wrong this time
articles.summary: NU looks driven to turn its early dominance into a championship after last year’s heartbreak, but UP remains close behind at the end of the UAAP men’s basketball first round

items: NU Bulldogs lead the UAAP Season 89 men's basketball tournament with a 5-2 record, aiming to avoid a repeat of last season's Final Four exit.
Head coach Jeff Napa emphasizes the need for consistency and maintaining high standards as the team prepares for the second round.
UP Fighting Maroons, also at 5-2, seek to improve after a strong finish to the first round, learning from both wins and losses as they aim for a return to the finals.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – NU boasts the best record again after the first round of eliminations in the UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball tournament. This time, however, the Bulldogs want to finish the job.
After topping last season’s eliminations, the Bulldogs suffered a Final Four exit, losing to eventual champion La Salle.

But the Bulldogs are determined to prove doubters wrong. NU head coach Jeff Napa knows consistency will be key, as well as the mindset that securing the No. 1 seed means little without a championship.

“We need to set standards. That’s what I told them, we needed to achieve in the first round,” Napa said in Filipino after the Bulldogs wrapped up the first round with a 69-65 win over the FEU Tamaraws for a 5-2 record.
“Heading into the second round, we need to remain consistent,” he added. “The players are proving to the doubters that they can compete in the UAAP.”
NU’s only losses came against the Ateneo Blue Eagles and La Salle Green Archers, both teams finishing tied for sixth place at 3-4.
The UP Fighting Maroons, another perennial title contender, also wound up with a 5-2 record, but NU gained the upper hand by winning their first-round meeting, 72-64.
Since falling to Ateneo, the Bulldogs have won three straight games, including an overtime thriller against the UST Growling Tigers and Adamson Soaring Falcons, who are both tied at 4-3.
Last season, NU ruled the elimination round with a league-best 11-3 record, but lost twice to La Salle in the semifinals.
Napa hopes that establishing a consistent standard of play will prevent a similar late-season collapse.

“Our mindset is that winners need to live up to the standards of winners,” Napa said. “We need to be consistent in everything we do. We shouldn’t relax just because we’re number one. We still have a long season ahead of us, and we have a lot of work to do.”
Unlike last season when NU could turn to Jake Figueroa in crucial moments, the Bulldogs have spread the scoring load more evenly this year.
MVP frontrunner Reinhard Jumamoy and PJ Palacielo have emerged as key contributors in a balanced offensive attack.
Jumamoy averaged 13.29 points per game and 5.14 assists per contest, the second-highest mark in the league during the first round.
Palacielo, meanwhile, posted averages of 12.0 points, 6.29 rebounds, and 4.43 assists per game.
NU also had three other double-digit scorers in Paul Francisco (10.86 points per game), Tebol Garcia (10.43), and foreign student-athlete Mo Diassana (10.29).
With the Bulldogs now carrying the league’s best record, Palacielo stressed that the team cannot afford to become complacent.
“It will be the same in the second round. We’ll stick to what our coaches, Coach Jeff (Napa) and the rest of the staff, prepare for us and focus on the roles they assign,” Palacielo said.
“We’re happy that we managed to get the win [against FEU], but we can’t afford to relax. We have to move forward and focus on the next game. This one is already behind us.”
Palacielo also emphasized the importance of having the entire roster ready to contribute, especially as the competition intensifies.
“All 16 players need to be ready whenever their number is called. Our primary players and those in Coach Jeff’s rotation won’t always have good games,” he said.
“We keep reminding them that if we want to reach the finals and become contenders, we need all 16 players to step up, not just the 10 players who usually see action on the court.”
After finishing the first round strong, UP also aims to stay consistent.
The loss to NU, followed by a defeat to FEU, served as a wake-up call for the Fighting Maroons, as they bounced back with wins over La Salle and UE to close out the round.
But their narrow escape against the winless Red Warriors showed there is still plenty of room for improvement.
UP allowed UE to dictate the pace for much of the game, with the Red Warriors building a lead of as many as 10 points before the Fighting Maroons rallied to avert a major upset.
For UP head coach Goldwin Monteverde, the comeback offered a valuable lesson ahead of the second round.
“Actually, UE got ahead of us in a way. That was a test for the team, having to come from behind and play tough defense to get back into the game,” Monteverde said.
“Along the way, of course, we need to learn how to start strong. I guess that’s something we’ll learn as we go through the season.”
Veejay Pre led UP in scoring during the first round, averaging 12.86 points, 6.43 rebounds, and 2.57 assists per game. Rey Remogat followed with 12.0 points per contest.
With another round ahead, Monteverde expects his players to learn from both their wins and losses as they pursue a return to the UAAP Finals for the sixth consecutive year.
“Good or bad experience, it’s still a good experience that will lead us toward our same goal,” Monteverde said.
UP will open the second round against UST on Wednesday, October 21, at the Mall of Asia Arena, while NU will face Adamson on Saturday, October 24, at the Blue Eagle Gym. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Senate resolution seeks to declare Chinese envoy ‘persona non grata’
articles.summary: The resolution also expresses the Senate’s 'serious concern' over Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan's controversial remarks

blocks.text: PH-CHINA TIES. In this file photo, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. summons Chinese ambassador Jing Quan 'over [a] maritime incident at Ayungin Shoal.'
Malacañang
The resolution also expresses the Senate’s 'serious concern' over Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan's controversial remarks

MANILA, Philippines – Senator Erwin Tulfo on Monday, October 19, filed a resolution seeking to declare Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan a “persona non grata” over his recent remarks, which the Philippine government described as a “thinly veiled threat of the use of force.”

In filing Senate Resolution No. 739, Tulfo expressed the Senate’s “serious concern” over the controversial statement of the Chinese envoy, who said China could easily defeat the Philippines if it resorted to using force.
“We should feel fortunate enough that you have a neighbor like China in this region. If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we’ll not use force. We love peace,” Jing said.
The Department of Foreign Affairs admonished Jing over his remarks. It also summoned the diplomat to express the government’s serious concern and strong objection to his public statement.

“It is hereby resolved by the Senate of the Philippines to express its serious concern over the remarks made by the Ambassador of China to the Philippines Jing Quan, suggesting the potential use of force against the Philippines,” the resolution read.

“Resolved further to urge the [Department of Foreign Affairs] to recommend to the appropriate authorities the declaration of Ambassador Jing Quan as persona non grata in view of the severity of his remarks and their implications for Philippine sovereignty, national dignity, and bilateral relations,” it said.

Senator JV Ejercito, over the weekend, first raised the possibility of senators filing a resolution to declare Jing persona non grata after the Chinese Embassy in Manila dared Philippine officials to do so.

“Some anti-China politicians talked about declaring the Chinese ambassador persona non grata (PNG). Over the past 30 years, anti-China forces have been repeatedly doing the same thing to threaten our embassy. We are fed up with these old and low tricks. If they really want to do something, do it quickly and immediately, please,” the embassy said.
“While diplomacy is based on reciprocity, we will not welcome them to China. Simple and fair enough,” it added.

Beijing claims almost all of the South China Sea, including areas part of the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone. China refuses to acknowledge the landmark 2016 Arbitral Award, which affirmed the Philippines’ EEZ and found China’s supposed historical claim invalid.

Under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., Manila has been both assertive and transparent in protecting both its sovereignty claims and rights in the West Philippine Sea. China’s claims have meant that, for Filipino frontliners — the Navy, Coast Guard, and even fisherfolk — harassment at the hands of Chinese maritime agencies is a risk in flashpoints in those waters.

After Monday’s filing, the Senate will discuss and vote on Tulfo’s resolution during the resumption of its plenary session on November 9. If approved, the upper chamber will adopt the resolution. – with reports from Bea Cupin/Rappler.com

articles.title: Third Ebola case in Kenya highlights US failures amid Trump cuts to key services
articles.summary:
Opposition to US-led quarantine center in Kenya follows sweeping funding cuts and withdrawal from WHO

A third person in Kenya has tested positive for Bundibugyo ebolavirus in the country’s…

blocks.text: A third person in Kenya has tested positive for Bundibugyo ebolavirus in the country’s first-ever cluster of Ebola cases, as the second-largest outbreak in history kills more than 4,300 and sickens more than 9,000 people in the region.

It highlights the diminished role the US has played in the worsening Ebola outbreak by building a controversial quarantine center in Kenya, pulling back health support globally, and banning travelers from certain countries. All of this has also reduced the ability to identify and respond to the outbreak and exacerbated mistrust.

The US created a controversial quarantine center at Kenya’s Laikipia air base, where Americans returning from the Democratic Republic of the Congo would be required to quarantine. The center, opposed by locals, has stirred distrust in the Kenyan government, leading to protests and a Kenyan court ordering a halt to the center.

“Many Kenyans were concerned about the fact that there was no information and people did not know why the quarantine place was being set up, who was actually going to use it, and what had informed that,” said Allan Maleche, executive director of the Kenya Legal & Ethical Issues Network on HIV and Aids (Kelin). The litigation will be decided in November, he said.
In the meantime, Kenyans are “very cautious around any information that is being given by the government around Ebola”, Maleche said.

Americans who questioned whether the US has the legal authority to quarantine Americans on foreign soil and prevent them from returning home are pushing back against the quarantine center as Kenya faces its first Ebola cases.

“Is this still a viable solution for the US?” asked Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the pandemic center at Brown University school of public health. “Are we posing not only an undue burden on the Kenyan government to be able to handle this, but also is this the safest place to be bringing Americans?”
The US already has “world-class” Ebola treatment units, Nuzzo pointed out.

“American taxpayers built these units for precisely this purpose, and it’s mind-boggling to me that we’re going to leave them empty,” she said. In previous outbreaks, actively ill patients have been evacuated safely to these centers, where they have recovered without further spread of the virus.

The unease follows sweeping cuts to US health support across the world, with the demolition of the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and cuts to funding and staff at health agencies like the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

On 1 October, the CDC closed HIV prevention offices in Angola and South Sudan, with plans to close offices in Zimbabwe. The US has slashed programs across the world – including DR Congo, where the Ebola outbreak is centered, and other countries, like Kenya, bracing for cases as the outbreak widens.
“We have had a lot of concerns after the US first cut funding for HIV promptly without any direction,” Maleche said. “It led to clinics closing. It led to a lot of anxiety among people.”

The US is now negotiating bilateral agreements with each country, including Kenya – a process that has been mired in secrecy, Maleche said. “It’s not very clear what’s the plan, who’s rolling it out, and what will be involved.”

Cuts to decades-long programs mean the affected countries and the US have less insight into what’s happening, in addition to a lessened ability to prevent and stop outbreaks. “When you pull back on those, not only do you leave those countries less prepared to deal with that day-to-day threat, but it also means that they’re less prepared to deal with future emergencies,” Nuzzo said.

The US officially left the World Health Organization (WHO) in January, making it much harder to collaborate on the response to crises like these. When the US left the WHO, it also “pulled out a substantial amount of funding”, said Maleche. That means the WHO’s response has also been “weakened”, he said.

A Kenyan man fell ill in DRC before traveling by road to Uganda and then flying to Nairobi on 3 October, where he died in a hospital two days later. On Wednesday, officials announced that a close contact – reportedly a 39-year-old man who is a family member of the first patient – developed symptoms while quarantining. And on Friday, officials announced a third case – a 65-year-old woman closely related to the first two patients.
Kenya’s ministry of health pointed to the success of contact tracing and quarantine. About 108 people have been quarantined in Nairobi.

“The general feeling is that the contact tracing systems are working,” Maleche said. But Kenyans are also wondering why there were “many lapses” that resulted in a sick person traveling across countries. The border between DRC and Uganda has been closed since May. Uganda was declared Ebola-free in August after earlier reporting 20 cases and two deaths.
A French doctor who returned from DRC in June tested positive, and several Americans have been evacuated from DRC to Europe for Ebola treatment or monitoring.

In Kenya, “the biggest fear is around how will other countries react” to the outbreak, with travel bans a particular worry, Maleche said. The US put travel bans in place from DRC and neighboring Uganda and South Sudan once the outbreak was detected in May, but it would be “very ironic” if the US instituted travel bans, given its quarantine center in Kenya, Maleche said.

Senator Raphael Warnock, a Democrat from Georgia, and Senator Bill Cassidy, a Republican from Louisiana, penned a letter in June to the Senate appropriations committee opposing the Trump administration’s plans to cut back on HIV prevention and monitoring.

Dismantling of USAID, withdrawing from the WHO, and abruptly cutting foreign aid cuts is “degrading our outbreak preparedness” and has “seriously weakened our ability to keep Americans safe from infectious disease”, Warnock said in a statement.

“These cuts to global health funding have led to the erosion of international disease-monitoring infrastructure that helps us catch threats like Ebola before they reach our shores, at a time when the world needs American leadership most.” The US should be strengthening these systems, not abandoning them, he said.

Nuzzo agreed. “It’s about having an understanding of the systems and the conditions in other countries, and eyes and ears in those countries to detect when something out of the ordinary happens, and to get that information as early as possible,” she said. That benefits the US and the countries themselves, she said.

Work like HIV prevention “can be repurposed”, she added. “You have connections with clinical care, the ability to move medicines, the ability to conduct laboratory tests. the ability to move specimens around – all of those capacities are things that you would use in other disease emergencies.”

articles.title: Who is Vice Admiral Rommel Supangan, the new PCG commandant?
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. formally appointed Vice Admiral Rommel Supangan on Monday as the new commandant of the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG).

blocks.text: Published October 19, 2026 7:56pm
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. formally appointed Vice Admiral Rommel Supangan on Monday as the new commandant of the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG).
Supangan replaces retired Admiral Ronnie Gil Gavan, who served as the 30th commandant of the PCG.
Before his appointment, Supangan served as the 25th Commander of the PCG Marine Environmental Protection Command (MEPCOM) from February to October 2026.

As MEPCOM commander, Supangan led the group in “expanding its engagements with government agencies, academic institutions, development partners, and maritime stakeholders, while advancing programs that strengthen marine environmental protection across the country,” the agency said.
Supangan also served as Commander of the Coast Guard Fleet from June 2025 to October 2026, and held the following positions within the PCG:

items: Director of the Coast Guard Strategic Studies and International Affairs Center
Commander of the Coast Guard Human Resource Management Command
Commander of Coast Guard District Palawan
Acting Commander of Coast Guard District NCR–Central Luzon
Deputy Commander of the Maritime Safety Services Command

blocks.text: With eight years of shipboard experience, Supangan is a holder of the Coast Guard Command-at-Sea Badge and a recipient of both the PMA Cavalier Award for Coast Guard Operations (Senior Officer Category) and the Coast Guard District Palawan Award.
Supangan previously commanded five Coast Guard commissioned vessels and two Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) vessels.
The new commandant is a member of the Philippine Military Academy “MARILAG” Class of 1995. He holds a Bachelor of Science degree in Naval Systems Engineering.

In 2008, he earned his master's degree in Maritime Affairs, majoring in Marine Environment and Ocean Management, from the World Maritime University in Malmö, Sweden, as a Sasakawa Fellow of the Nippon Foundation. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Personal attacks fire up debate before Brazil's run-off vote
articles.summary: The race heats up just days before the run-off between the left-wing incumbent and his right-wing challenger.

blocks.text: Brazil's left-wing President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his right-wing rival, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, have clashed in a debate held one week before the run-off presidential election.
Polls suggest the two candidates are neck and neck and the televised debate was hailed as a chance for both to sway undecided voters.
But the showdown was marked by personal attacks and analysts have warned that its aggressive tone may increase the abstention rate further.
In the first round of voting, held on 4 October, Bolsonaro defied opinion polls by securing a narrow lead over Lula.
Sunday's debate was the first of two before the vote. The second is planned for Friday, just two days before polls open.

Flávio Bolsonaro is standing for the Liberal Party after his father, Jair Bolsonaro - who governed from 2018 to 2022 - was sentenced to more than 20 years in prison for plotting to overthrow Lula after the latter beat him in the 2022 election.
The younger Bolsonaro won 47% of the vote in the first round, compared with Lula's 45.2%, with both falling short of the 50% of the valid votes needed to stave off a decisive second round.

Since the return to democracy in 1988, there has been no instance in which the candidate who lost in the first round went on to win in the second but Lula has told his supporters that he will "win in extra time".
Analysts consulted by BBC News Brasil were struck by how much the debate was dominated not by issues but personal attacks.
Yuri Sanches from pollsters AtlasIntel said it was a debate in which no policies were discussed and there were no rational arguments.
"The independent voter, who is sometimes against Bolsonaro and sometimes against the Workers' Party [of Lula], came out of it with a very negative impression."
Lucas Aragão from political analysis firm Arko Advice said Bolsonaro had appeared calmer during the debate and seemed to have managed to "get under Lula's skin".

Rafael Cortez from consulting firm da Tendências Consultoria, however, argued that Lula had managed to score a goal when he said he would open up his financial and phone records and those of his family to judicial scrutiny, and challenged his rival to do the same before Sunday's run-off.
Many observers criticised the format of the debate, which was described as chaotic at times, with each of the candidates pacing around the TV studio as the other was speaking.
One heated exchange saw Bolsonaro telling Lula he should come stand next to him so that the two could talk.

Referring to alleged links between the senator and paramilitary vigilante groups, Lula said "I don't want to be close to you", and that he wanted to maintain "distance from the Bolsonaro family" and "the militia".
Bolsonaro, who has dismissed the allegations as fake news, in turn tried to bait Lula by saying, "On second thoughts, maybe it's better to keep my distance so that my wallet isn't stolen."
He also accused the Workers' Party of being corrupt, holding up the palm of his hand on which he had scribbled "CORRUPTO" (Portuguese for "corrupt).
"Take a piece of paper and a pen and jot down 'corrupt' and you'll see that it has two letters in the middle here together," he said, pointing to PT, the initials of the Workers' Party in Portuguese.
Bolsonaro, who is campaigning on a iron-fist approach to crime, challenged Lula to explain why crime rates had gone up during his four years in power.
He also alleged, without providing any evidence, that "the majority of convicts vote for Lula".
Lula shot back with a thinly veiled reference to Flávio's convicted father, Jair, saying; "I wish it was 100%, even your father".

articles.title: UN food program cuts aid to 500,000 Palestinians in Gaza
articles.summary: Amid funding shortages, the World Food Program has said it is being forced to reduce necessary aid. Over two-thirds of Palestinians in Gaza are facing acute hunger, according to the agency.

image.caption: The cut to aid comes with winter approaching and no end in sight for the conflictImage: Jehad Alshrafi/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) has been forced to cut its monthly food aid to the war-ravaged Gaza Strip , where some two-thirds of the population are struggling to get food, the agency said on Monday.
The WFP said it was reducing the number of people receiving aid from 1.6 million to 1.1 million, leaving some 500,000 people without support.
The UN program is facing severe funding shortages. "WFP no longer has sufficient funding to sustain this level of support," the organization said.
What UN aid is being cut in Gaza?
Beyond the cutting of aid to some half a million recipients in the region, the WFP is also:

items: Reducing rations by half
Cash assistance has been cut for some 75,000 families
Hot meals for those unable to cook have been reduced from 250,000 to 150,000

blocks.text: Some 1.4 million people in Gaza are facing crisis levels of food insecurity according to the WFP, with 200,000 living in emergency conditions.
Despite a US-brokered ceasefire that came into effect last year, Israeli strikes have continued and aid has remained restricted, with little progress toward a final end to the conflict.

"It's a year into the agreement of this ceasefire. Well, life is still brutal here. There is no proper shelter. There is no ⁠basic ​services. There is no safety, no security," acting Executive ​Director of the World Food Program WFP Carl Skau told Reuters in Gaza.
"These cuts are happening ​just as we are facing the fourth winter. You know, I've been through the winters here, absolutely brutal," he added.
Gaza's children bear lasting scars three years into war
Why is aid being cut to Gaza?
The UN program urgently needs $450 million (€400 million) to keep funding its critical operations in Gaza and the West Bank over the next six months.

"We tell the world now ⁠is not ​the time to look away. This is the time to step up to sustain this support, to protect the progress that has been made, but also to push for early recovery," Skau said.
The WFP had already announced cuts to aid for the West Bank in early September, citing funding shortages and donor fatigue.

The Israeli authority responsible for the Palestinian territories, COGAT, says the supply of aid deliveries into the strip exceeds the demand for food and it claims there is no acute food insecurity in Gaza.

articles.title: DOH aims to vaccinate over 2M students vs HPV under Bakuna Eskwela
articles.summary: The Department of Health (DOH) on Monday said it aims to vaccinate two million students against Human Papillomavirus (HPV), a virus that causes cervical cancer, under the Bakuna Eskwela program.

blocks.text: Published October 19, 2026 7:37pm
The Department of Health (DOH) on Monday said it aims to vaccinate two million students against Human Papillomavirus (HPV), a virus that causes cervical cancer, under the Bakuna Eskwela program.
"Our target for HPV is around 2.007 million learners from Grades 4 and 5 from public and private schools,” Alethea de Guzman, DOH Epidemiology Bureau director, said in a virtual media briefing.
“And of these approximately two million learners, around nine percent are estimated to be out-of-school youth,” she added.
Bakuna Eskwela is an annual school-based immunization program of DOH and the Department of Education.
The ongoing immunization program offers vaccines against cervical cancer, measles, German measles (rubella), tetanus, and diphtheria.
As of 2022, there are 7,829 cervical cancer cases recorded in the Philippines, De Guzman said.

According to the World Health Organization, the top five cancers in the Philippines are breast (28,124 cases), colorectal (7,899 cases), cervical uteri (7,829 cases), thyroid (6,450 cases), and corpus uteri (5,626 cases).
De Guzman also called for raising awareness about cervical cancer and its prevention.

"Alam natin ang mga nanay, tatay, ‘yung mga caregivers naman ang nagde-decide para sa ating learners and we encourage them, we empower them to have the right information and hopefully, with that, they consent so that their children payagan na po talaga na mabigyan po ng HPV vaccine po natin," she said.

(We know that parents and caregivers make decisions on behalf of our learners. We encourage and empower them with the right information so they can give their consent and allow their children to receive the HPV vaccine.)

Nelinda Catherine Pangilinan, specialty center head of Rizal Medical Center, earlier said reproductive health should be included in the basic education curriculum, as more cases of cervical cancer have been observed among young Filipino patients.

"What we want is to have an education campaign or a curriculum to include how to take care of oneself, and at the same time, sexual reproduction or reproductive health that should be incorporated already in the curriculum," Pangilinan told reporters.
She said Filipino patients as young as 20 years old have been diagnosed with cervical cancer.
Some of the patients were found to have engaged in sexual intercourse as young as 14 years old and have had three or more sexual partners.

"I do not know if it might be in the trend right now, or the value of sex is just part of a common activity," Pangilinan said, adding that cervical cancer is usually diagnosis to patients 30 years old and above. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Italian PM Meloni to hold emergency meeting after weekend of violent clashes
articles.summary: More than 200 people were detained during two days of rioting in the city, Italian media reports.

blocks.text: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is set to hold an emergency security meeting on Monday after protests over the rising cost of living broke out into violent clashes in Milan.
More than 5,000 people gathered over the weekend. Police deployed tear gas and water cannons after protesters - many in masks - threw paving stones, bins and chairs at officers.
"To demonstrate is a right. To lay our cities to waste is not," Meloni said on Saturday, adding that "hooligans" had exploited the protests to "sow chaos".
Rioting and violence have broken out on the sidelines of mostly peaceful youth-led protests in other European countries including France, Spain and Albania.
Milanese Mayor Giuseppe Sala said he was worried it was a "new phenomenon" that "originates from an international scenario and therefore feeds itself".

Speaking to Italian news agency Ansa, he said he witnessed "smashed shop windows, looted stores, and frightened citizens", adding that "what happened here is what we are seeing in many cities around the world".
Clashes began on Saturday and continued into Sunday in Milan. More than 200 people were detained, 80% of whom were minors, Ansa reported.
The city's prosecutor's office has requested prison sentences for five adults arrested for looting, vandalism and resisting arrest, according to Italian news agency AGI.
Italian media reported that people - including police officers - were injured.
Violence between protesters and police also rippled into other cities in the north.
Meloni said people in Turin were detained while "carrying cobblestones and window-breaking hammers", while a train station in Bologna was closed as a precaution after similar disorder.
The prime minister - who is facing an election next year - also called on her political opponents to condemn the rioting.
"Do not be ambiguous about this," she said on X, explaining that condemnation must be "unanimous" because "any hesitation becomes justification".

Democratic Party leader Elly Schlein said her party had always condemned violence and that the rioting should not be used to stifle the voices of peaceful protesters across the country who are struggling to make a living, Ansa reported.

The violent disorder followed anti-government protests held by students in various Italian cities on Friday, and echoed similar unrest in neighbouring France, where hundreds of thousands took to the streets.

image.caption: A sign for advance voting, which began Oct. 5. Twenty-one candidates are running for eight city council seats, while two candidates are running for mayor. (Carson Asmundson/CBC)

blocks.text: North
Today is voting day for the Yellowknife municipal elections, as well as the trustee elections for two school boards in the city.
5 voting stations open across the city from 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.
Voters in Yellowknife will be selecting a new mayor and council Monday, as well as trustees for school boards.
On Monday night, CBC North will be running a live page where you can follow the results, news and analysis. Reporters will be in the field talking to candidates throughout the night.
There are 21 candidates running for city council, of which the top eight will be elected, and two running for mayor.

items: We had questions for Yellowknife's council candidates. Here's what they had to say
Q&A | Yellowknife mayoral candidate Melissa Syer on her vision for the city
Q&A | Yellowknife mayoral candidate Garett Cochrane on his vision for the city

The city is offering free transit to voting stations Monday and extending transit hours for the election.
You can read more about the candidates running for Yellowknife District 1 and the Yellowknife Catholic Schools.

articles.title: Senate panel endorses DENR's P28-B budget for 2027
articles.summary: A Senate Finance subcommittee on Monday endorsed to the plenary the proposed P28.04-billion budget of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) and its attached agencies for 2027.

blocks.text: Published October 19, 2026 6:58pm
A Senate Finance subcommittee on Monday endorsed to the plenary the proposed P28.04-billion budget of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) and its attached agencies for 2027.
In his presentation, DENR Secretary Juan Miguel Cuna said P20.62 billion of the proposed budget would go to the department’s central office, staff bureaus, regional offices and other smaller offices.

The remaining funds would be allocated as follows: P3.10 billion for the Environmental Management Bureau (EMB), P1.98 billion for the National Mapping and Resource Information Authority (NAMRIA), P1.89 billion for the Mines and Geosciences Bureau (MGB), P284.35 million for the National Water Resources Board (NWRB) and P149.3 million for the Palawan Council for Sustainable Development Staff (PCSDS).

Aside from the DENR’s proposed programs and projects for next year, Sen. Risa Hontiveros, who led the budget hearing, urged the department to prioritize preparedness and emergency response measures against the threat of a super El Niño.

“Hindi pwedeng taumbayan lang ang mag-aadjust (the public shouldn’t be the only ones expected to adjust). DENR must step up to a historic challenge. It will be a critical and leading agency in the government’s response to this looming risk of widespread drought," Hontiveros said.
"The agency’s work will have real, tangible implications for the economy, health and daily living conditions of millions,” she added.
Hontiveros stressed that the DENR’s budget should adequately fund preparations and emergency response measures to mitigate the impact of the looming drought on Filipinos.
“Filipino people expect agility in the response and fitness for purpose of the budgets of frontline agencies such as the DENR. Its budget should reflect this," she said.
"Dapat buhusan ng pondo ang paghahanda at emergency response sa paparating na tagtuyot para maibsan ang dagok nito sa bawat Pilipino,” Hontiveros added.
(Funds must be allocated for preparations and emergency response to the looming drought to mitigate its impact on every Filipino.)

Hontiveros also called for funding for small water impoundment systems to collect and store rainwater for use during droughts. She said available technologies, such as atmospheric water stations developed by the Local Water Utilities Administration, should also be tapped to identify alternative sources of potable water.
Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano, meanwhile, called for stronger environmental education in elementary and high school curricula.

He said the DENR should work closely with the Department of Education (DepEd) and the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) to ensure that practical lessons on ecology and conservation are integrated into school curricula.

Sen. Pia Cayetano likewise urged the DENR to collaborate with education agencies to ensure that environmental education addresses the specific needs of coastal and mountainous communities.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: From delivery driver to global fame: A Korean writer's journey
articles.summary: You Yeong-Gwang's The Rainfall Market tells the story of a mysterious, hidden shop that only opens when it rains. For a debut novel by an unknown author, it was a massive success.

image.caption: The book was a massive success, securing publication in 15 languages, including English, German, Spanish and ChineseImage: ClayHouse/Michael Joseph/Ace

blocks.text: For ten years, publishers rejected You Yeong-Gwang's book. Yet before it was even printed in South Korea, the once-abandoned manuscript had international publishers flocking to secure translation rights.

"I'm so grateful that the book has now been published in more than 20 countries. Even more astonishingly, it also appeared on the Der Spiegel bestseller list in Germany," he told DW while attending the 2026 Frankfurt Book Fair.
For a debut novel by an unknown author, it was a massive success, securing publication in 15 languages, including English, German, Spanish and traditional Chinese.

The Rainfall Market tells the story of a mysterious, hidden shop that only opens when it rains. In the shop, visitors can exchange their deepest unhappiness for a ticket to a brand-new destiny. The plot revolves around Serin, a disheartened young girl who stumbles into the marketplace run by whimsical spirits, finding a warm, comforting space.
"In fact, Serin's story is my story," author You said. "For a long time, I even wondered how wonderful it would be if I could sell my unhappiness and use the money to buy happiness."
While writing the book, he was going through a difficult time himself.
"I had to care for my mother, who had been ill for a long time, and I had also been responsible for supporting my family financially for many years. Life felt incredibly heavy," he reflected.

"But when I was writing, I could immerse myself in the world of the story and, even if only for a short while, forget about those circumstances. That's why writing made me so happy. I truly enjoyed it."
On the creation of The Rainfall Market
The idea of rain is inspired by his own life. "At that time, my circumstances felt as though it were raining constantly," You said.

blocks.caption: You Yeong-gwang, author of 'The Rainfall Market'Image: ClayHouse

blocks.text: The story draws heavily on traditional Korean folklore, serving as a quintessential "healing fiction" tale in which its young protagonist must weigh the true cost of seemingly perfect lives.
"When I was writing, I wasn't consciously trying to write healing fiction. At the time, I didn't even really know that such a label existed."

He initially planned to publish a book independently and started crowdfunding. But as the funding failed, he used all his savings and printed 200 copies, which bookstores refused to take. In a month, he only sold five copies. "I thought that's it. I really have to give up now.”

"At the time, I had undergone eye surgery and due to complications, I couldn't see, so I started working at a call center, where I could work using my voice." You said. "During the week, I worked at a call center, and on weekends I went to a computer academy. I learned how to make books on my own for a few years."
He then taught himself how to use the software needed to create books on his own.

While running one of the crowdfunding campaigns, he started working as a food delivery rider. "The round trip between my home and the area where I delivered food took about four hours each day. So I wrote on my phone's memo app while traveling on the subway."

"Even when I was going through very difficult circumstances, I was able to keep writing because the moments when I was writing were so joyful. For a little while, I could forget about the difficult situation I was in," You explained.
Finally a breakthrough
"I gathered those pieces of writing together and launched what I intended to be my final crowdfunding campaign," he said.
The campaign was intended to fund the publication of The Rainfall Market.
"To my amazement, the campaign succeeded, and I was able to publish the book commercially for the first time," he said.
How K-pop pushes appetite for Korean ramyun noodles
Following the crowdfunding success, the novel was acquired by Clayhouse, a prominent South Korean publishing company.
Before it was even published, he had received offers from publishers in five countries and signed international publishing contracts.
And in the first month after publication, the book sold 30,000 copies across all formats, ranking as the bestselling e-book and third-bestselling physical book.
"I still find it hard to believe that all of this has happened and that I'm here at the Frankfurt Book Fair. I'm incredibly grateful and happy," said You.
A new horizon for Hallyu, or the 'Korean Wave': K-Comfort Fiction
Korea's newest soft power is K-literature, which sold about 1.2 million translated copies abroad in 2025 for the second consecutive year.
And You's book belongs to a trending genre called Korean comfort fiction.
"When readers closed the book, I wanted them to feel a little warmth in their hearts," he said.

Although Korean literature was first known for darker, more pragmatic books about societal realities, K-comfort fiction is the child of South Korea's pressure-cooker modern society. It offers an answer to the human need for escapism and a transient antidote to the reality of a hyper-competitive education system, brutal job market, and intense corporate pressure.

"When I was writing, I was going through a very difficult time myself, and I wished someone would comfort me. So, I thought, why don't I try reading something like that myself? Why don't I write something that can comfort me?" You wondered.

With burnout on the rise globally, more readers are seeking soul-soothing literature with exhausted protagonists they can relate to. Usually without a need to defeat a villain, the stories follow protagonists with a deep desire for rest, community and emotional repair.

The whimsical fiction aspect is the missing element allowing them to step away from reality. The genre originally gained traction through indie productions, online crowdfunding and endorsements from high-profile K-pop artists.
How South Korea is cashing in on 'KPop Demon Hunters'

Despite the Korean context, this style of storytelling quickly went global, capturing different international audiences, including those already familiar with cozy K-dramas or those simply looking for a gentle refuge from the anxieties of the modern world.

Last year, the bestselling Korean novel abroad was Welcome to the Hyunam-dong Bookshop, according to the Literature Translation Institute of Korea. This book also belongs to the same genre as The Rainfall Market.

While readers embrace the genre, critics view it with literary skepticism. They point out that it relies heavily on a predictable, repetitive formula, often built around a single magical space, with simplistic prose and low-stakes conflicts that prioritize cozy vibes over deep character development.

Reviewing The Rainfall Market for the Korea Times, Peter Juhl, a literary critic, described healing fiction as light, feel-good stories and argued the boom reflects a deliberate effort to write global novels for international markets.
On his future aspirations and message to readers

"Of course, I'm happy that my book is receiving so much love and that I'm able to write. But more than anything, I hope my mother gets better and regains her health," he said after mentioning that his mother underwent surgery a week before his arrival at the book fair.
Beyond the book itself, people seem to relate to and appreciate the story of his own life.

"If I have the opportunity, I'd like to share more stories about hope and dreams with people who are going through circumstances similar to mine," said You. "If my story can help one person even a little, in any way, I don't think anything could make me happier."

articles.title: Champi now a super typhoon again ahead of entry into PAR
articles.summary: The trough or extension of Super Typhoon Champi may already trigger scattered rain and thunderstorms in Catanduanes, Northern Samar, and Eastern Samar, says PAGASA on Monday afternoon, October 19

blocks.text: CHAMPI. Satellite image of Super Typhoon Champi outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility as of October 19, 2026, 4 pm.
PAGASA
The trough or extension of Super Typhoon Champi may already trigger scattered rain and thunderstorms in Catanduanes, Northern Samar, and Eastern Samar, says PAGASA on Monday afternoon, October 19

items: Champi re-intensified into a super typhoon outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility, with maximum sustained winds of 185 km/h.
The super typhoon remains on track to enter PAR by Tuesday, October 20.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Champi re-intensified into a super typhoon on Monday afternoon, October 19, ahead of its expected entry into the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR).

Champi’s maximum sustained winds increased from 175 kilometers per hour to 185 km/h, said the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) in an advisory issued at 5 pm on Monday. Its gustiness is now up to 230 km/h from the previous 215 km/h.
The super typhoon was located 1,515 kilometers east of southeastern Luzon as of 4 pm, moving west northwest at a slightly slower 15 km/h from 20 km/h.
It is still projected to enter PAR by Tuesday morning or early afternoon, October 20. Upon entry, it will be given the local name Rosal.

PAGASA said Champi will continue to move west northwest until Wednesday, October 21, before moving generally northwest starting Thursday, October 22. It is likely to stay over the Philippine Sea, where it could strengthen further before gradually weakening Thursday onwards.

Even before Champi enters PAR, its trough or extension may already trigger scattered rain and thunderstorms in Catanduanes, Northern Samar, and Eastern Samar in the coming hours. Flash floods and landslides are possible.

The super typhoon could be closest to the Philippines’ northernmost province of Batanes on Friday, October 23. It is expected to bring heavy rain to extreme Northern Luzon, or the Batanes-Babuyan Islands area, even though it is unlikely to make landfall.

Tropical cyclone wind signals might also be raised for the northern and eastern portions of Northern Luzon and even parts of Bicol as early as Monday evening or Tuesday morning. The weather bureau’s latest forecast shows Signal No. 2 or 3 could be the highest, while Signal No. 4 is no longer seen as a possibility.
PAGASA added that most parts of Luzon and the Visayas, as well as portions of Mindanao, are likely to experience gusty conditions beginning Wednesday.
As for coastal conditions, moderate to rough waters are expected in the northern and eastern seaboards of Luzon and the eastern seaboards of the Visayas and Mindanao on Tuesday.
Starting Wednesday, very rough, high, or very high waters may affect the northern and eastern seaboards of Luzon.
Champi may exit PAR by Saturday, October 24.

blocks.text: Aside from the trough of the super typhoon, other sources of rain in the coming hours include the intertropical convergence zone (ITCZ) and the easterlies.
The ITCZ is a belt near the equator where the trade winds of the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere meet, while the easterlies are warm winds from the Pacific Ocean.

Scattered rain and thunderstorms will persist in the Zamboanga Peninsula and Palawan due to the ITCZ, while isolated rain showers or thunderstorms may hit Cagayan Valley, the Cordillera Administrative Region, and the Ilocos Region because of the easterlies.
The Philippines is currently in a transition period to the northeast monsoon or amihan, following the end of the southwest monsoon or habagat, which was announced last October 5.

The northeast monsoon typically brings surges of cold temperatures, but the upcoming amihan period could be warmer as the existing strong El Niño in the tropical Pacific Ocean is predicted to become very strong in the fourth quarter of 2026. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Congress mourns LP stalwart, Martial Law survivor Raul Daza
articles.summary: Lawmakers on Monday mourned the passing of lifelong Liberal Party stalwart and former Northern Samar governor Raul Daza, who died last week at the age of 91.

blocks.text: Lawmakers on Monday mourned the passing of lifelong Liberal Party stalwart and former Northern Samar governor Raul Daza, who also represented the province at the House of Representatives at several times over the decades, including during the Martial Law regime and after the 1986 People Power revolution.

At the necrological service at the Batasang Pambansa, House Deputy Speaker Ferdinand Hernandez of South Cotabato called Daza a lifelong fighter for democracy. He recounted that Daza was a Liberal Party lawmaker who opposed President Ferdinand Marcos Sr.'s Martial Law regime, then became a Deputy Commissioner of the Presidential Commission on Good Government under the administration of President Corazon Aquino and a member of the House as Northern Samar Representative in the 8th, 9th, 10th, 15th, 16th, and 17th Congresses.

“In these capacities, he brought his extensive experience in legislation and governance closer to the communities whose welfare remained central to his life's work. He was steadfast in his principles, demonstrating a consistency of conviction that endured to the changing political circumstances and successive administrations,” Hernandez said.

“His legislative contributions reflected this conviction that the meaningful progress must be measured not simply by the laws enacted, by the opportunities they create and the lives they improved,” Hernandez added.

Some of the laws authored by Daza under Republic Act 6639, which renamed the Manila International Airport the Ninoy Aquino International Airport; Republic Act number 8291, or the Government Service Insurance System Act of 1997; and Republic Act 8544, which regulates the merchant marine profession in the Philippines.
Daza died on October 12 at the age of 91.

Former House Deputy Speaker Erin Tañada III also shared that while then-House Deputy Speaker Daza did oppose the passage of the Reproductive Health Law in Congress in 2012, a priority bill of President Benigno “Noynoy” Aquino III's administration, Daza did not use his position to delay the passage of the measure.

“Although he had his own convictions, he did not want to use his authority of the Speaker's gavel to obstruct the legislative process. He asked me to step in and preside whenever the bill was taken up. He didn't want to use the gavel to obstruct the legislative process. Think about the significance of that decision. Manong Raul did not abandon his principles,” Tañada said.

“He did not pretend to agree with something that conflicted with his own personal beliefs. He remained faithful to his convictions. But he also recognized that in a democracy, public service requires respect for institutions, for the legislative process, and for the legitimate will of the majority. He understood that holding a position of authority does not give us the right to use that authority to frustrate every decision with which we disagree,” he added.
Simple, meaningful gestures

House Deputy Minority Leader of Leila de Lima of ML party-list also recalled the times Daza paid her a visit during the times she was detained on drug charges where she was ultimately acquitted of, saying Daza faced the same persecution during the Marcos Martial law years.

“During my imprisonment, Manong Raul visited me in 2018 and also in 2019. He would occasionally send me books, letters, and rosaries. To some, this might seem like simple gestures, but to someone, for someone, whose freedom has been deprived of, that would come to understand, would understand how much, how much a familiar voice, a thoughtful letter, and a visit from an old friend can mean,” de Lima said.

“Manong Raul had known persecution himself. He lived through the dictatorship. He spent years in exile and returned to the Philippines despite the risk. I believe that experience gave him a particular understanding, what it meant to stand by someone during difficult times. And I will always be grateful that he stood by me,” she added.
Senator Risa Hontiveros, for her part, lauded Daza for standing up for what is right, no matter the costs and hearing out even those who are way younger than him.

“Manong Raul was a patriot who loved our country. He could have stayed in the United States where he had already won asylum [during the Marcos Martial Law era], but in the face of a standing warrant of arrest here, he chose to come back and fight. From a safer place, he moved back into the line of fire, getting arrested, being incarcerated, then joining the parliament of the streets and winning higher honor in our eyes,” Hontiveros said.

“An infinitely political animal, he sought the wise, even the purposes of such efforts, even from younger allies like me, in order to take his principal position on them as he had done at many other critical junctures of our nation's history. Raul Daza is a small boy who would not be bullied, who took up boxing to put muscle behind that resolve and who punched upward all throughout his life. He had a kind heart who gave as good as he got in the struggles of our times,” she added. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: The homeless man living in front of a London mega-mansion
articles.summary: Anders Fernstedt lives in London without any money. The Swedish native has built a most unusual home under the porch of a house worth over €200 million. How did that happen?

image.caption: Anders Fernstedt has built a home outside one of London's most expensive propertiesImage: Dan Redding/DW

blocks.text: There's a lot of stopping and staring in Knightsbridge. This part of central London is within a stone's throw of Buckingham Palace, Hyde Park and Harrods, bringing inquisitive tourists in droves.

While it may not divert quite as many eyeballs as the seat of the British monarchy, a curious collection of plants, garden umbrellas, shopping bags and children's toys filling a building's entrance causes many a curious glance.
The peculiar arrangement on a grand portico is what Anders Fernstedt, a man from Sweden who fell on hard times, has been calling home for more than three years already.
That building hosting his makeshift setup was, just a few years ago, London's most expensive house.

The mega-mansion at 2-8A Rutland Gate sold in 2020 for a then-record £210 million (€244 million, $278 million) to Hui Ka Yan, the founder of China's Evergrande group, who was sentenced to life in prison last month.
Hui never moved in and the house was registered under his wife's name. The freezing of her assets means it can't be seized by liquidators and the house is in a state of limbo.
Chinese court hands Evergrande property tycoon life sentence
So too was Fernstedt when he first stumbled across it. "I just thought, it would be a shelter for the night. I'm an avid camper, like an amateur botanist. I'm not afraid of nature," he told DW.
'Camping on the balcony'

Fernstedt has never been inside the property, which appears to be in a state of disrepair. Instead, he gradually built his home in the portico, where grand columns guard the 45 rooms, indoor swimming pool and 116 windows. Year round he sleeps under the portico roof and a large umbrella which provides a hidden nook in which he's placed mattresses and bedding.
"I haven't had a bad night's sleep for as long as I can remember. And that goes for four seasons. It's not cold in the winter, and because I don't have walls, I get the breeze in the heat," he said.
"My conceit when I started was that sort of fake dream. Oh, I'm just a boy, my parents are in the house, everything's normal, I just asked them for permission to camp on the balcony."

blocks.caption: 2-8A Rutland Gate sold for €244 million in 2020 but has been unoccupied sinceImage: Dan Redding/DW

blocks.text: Fernstedt was raised by his mother in Sweden before embarking on a range of careers at home and in the US, building a name for himself in the tech world.
In 2016, he moved to England where he worked as a journalist and fact checker at publications including The Economist, before work dried up around the time of the COVID pandemic.

A share in a tech company from his days in the US gave Anders a nest egg he relied on. But it couldn't last forever and he found himself living in a tent and then temporary accommodation, where he experienced violence and brushed up against people with severe addictions.
"Perhaps in this contemporary world, the biggest curiosity about my lifestyle is I'm completely off money," he said.
Community support powers unusual lifestyle

Fernstedt has built relationships with bakeries, cafes and florists in which he gets unused food, flowers for his home and use of power. He also makes use of a homeless charity in nearby Victoria for showers, clothing donations and socializing. But he's also made himself a broadly accepted part of one of London's most affluent neighborhoods.

blocks.caption: Fernstedt's home evolved over several years, through donations and giftsImage: Dan Redding/DW

blocks.text: "This is a very sophisticated neighborhood. I'd stayed for a few weeks and I knew everybody knew that I was here. And I thought, how can I sort of convey my presence without being present? And I thought, my constituency has to be the neighbors' children and grandchildren. Because if they plead my case at the kitchen table, my prospects improve," he said, by way of explaining the toys that line his abode.

"It is, in a way, a squirrel's nut collection," he added, when asked if he's worried about leaving his possessions out in the open. "I have so many nuts that I won't notice when something disappears."

There are some neighbors who do object to his presence, but Anders does his best to keep his home neat and his life quiet. Indeed, many others feel his presence prevents the house being a target for thieves or vandals. Overall though, he's found the community welcoming.

"Sometimes they introduce themselves asking what might I want or need. And my stock answer being: 'well, what you just gave me, a little bit of normal time, right? And neighborly banter'," he said. "Sometimes I'll be given food and very elegant Italian dinner jackets and clothes have arrived on a few occasions."
Homelessness a growing concern in London

Not all homeless people in London have found such a stable lifestyle. Homeless charity Crisis estimates that there are over 200,000 people classified as homeless in England's capital, where "4,392 people were recorded sleeping rough in London between April and June, up from 4% on the same time last year. This is up 58% compared to 10 years ago."

According to government figures, there were 105,138 empty homes in London in 2025, or 1 in every 37 homes. Andy Burnham, who became British Prime Minister in July, has since vowed to offer "every rough sleeper in England a route off the streets by Christmas."
Britain's new PM takes on fight against homelessness
With such an enormous price tag, even after six years of being abandoned, Fernstedt knows that the house he lives at could potentially become untenable at virtually any moment.
But over the last few years, it's given him something he craved when pitching up his tent or being moved from one scary temporary residence to the next.
"I'm no longer really worried that I'll cycle around the corner and everything will be gone. Because I've been here so long, I'm free of worrying now, and if we worry too much, we won't be happy."

articles.title: AMLC: Manila court orders forfeiture of funds linked to terrorism financing
articles.summary: A Manila court has ordered the forfeiture of funds linked to terrorism financing, the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) said on Monday.

blocks.text: Published October 19, 2026 6:31pm
A Manila court has ordered the forfeiture of funds linked to terrorism financing, the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) said on Monday.

The AMLC said the Manila Regional Trial Court (RTC) Branch 18 ordered the forfeiture of P217,165 previously held in a bank account belonging to Abdulpatta Escalon Abubakar, who has been linked to terrorism financing activities.
“The successful forfeiture demonstrates the indispensable role of financial intelligence and asset recovery measures in disrupting terrorism financing,” the AMLC said in a statement.
“By depriving terrorist facilitators of access to funds and financial services, authorities can impede their ability to plan, support and sustain terrorist activities,"
The AMLC said that the forfeiture supposedly underscored the importance of financial investigations in the country’s efforts to combat terrorism financing.

According to the AMLC, law enforcement authorities had reported that Abubakar facilitated the transfer of funds from Saudi Arabia to the Philippines through the wives and relatives of members of the Abu Sayyaf Group (ASG).

It added that Abubakar had been designated as a terrorist under United Nations Security Council Resolution 1267 for allegedly acting as a facilitator for the Islamic State in Iraq and the Levant (ISIL).
The AMLC also said international authorities had identified Abubakar as a key facilitator who transferred US$50,000 to Isnilon Hapilon, a former ASG leader.

The funds were believed to have been used to acquire weapons and ammunition. Abubakar was also linked to efforts to procure materials for manufacturing improvised explosive devices, the AMLC said. — MCG, GMA News
